The mountain and the oyster are the same teaching. The irritation is the material. The altitude is the choice. And the pearl, like the view above the clouds, was available all along to anyone willing to climb.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Still Pool
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the still pool.

Tonight's story is about a young man who wanted only one thing. Not food, not rest, not companionship. He was weary of the ways of the world, and he sought only the knowledge of the Creator.

He asked everyone. One great teacher told him the Creator was a vastness apart from this little life, which is called heaven. Another said the Creator lurked in running water and was in fact a state of nothingness. A third, very convincing, taught that the Creator was honor and righteousness and a graceful way of life. Each answer made a certain sense. None of them satisfied him.

So he looked to nature instead, to the stars and the forests and the seas, since no man, however wise, could tell him what he needed to know. And one day, sitting beside a still pool, he was joined by a very old man, with little hair and little height, his clothes tattered, who smiled and sat down beside him and asked after his health.

I am quite well, stranger, said the young man, but my heart is heavy. The things of this world do not satisfy me, and yet I cannot find that which is more permanent. I cannot understand the Creator. The old man nodded, pointed at the still pool, and said, have a look into the water, for there is the beginning and the end of your search. And then he was gone, leaving the young wanderer gazing at his own face in the calm, clear water.

There is every reason, Hatonn says, in the illusion you inhabit, to believe the truth will come to you from outside yourself. Everyone around you believes all things come from the outside. There are things you can purchase. You can learn how to make the illusion work. But what you cannot purchase at any price, from outside yourself, is the knowledge of why things are as they are, why you are here, and what is the nature of your being.

To look in the mirror, he says, is to see an infinitely small part of the creation, and this creation, to the best of our knowledge, is made entirely of love. Within that image in the mirror lie depths you can only see with great desire and discipline, for what you seek within yourself is locked within you like a seed within the earth, or a babe in the womb. It is through quietness and confidence and meditation that the seed germinates and the babe is born. That entity, he says, is the part of yourself that is most fully the original Thought of the Creator. The original Thought of love.

The questions that night circled the practical side of seeking. Someone asked whether astral projection was a genuine achievement or merely a trick of the mind, and the answer gives you a test you can use for any pursuit. Ask yourself, Hatonn says, how may I serve others through this activity? If you can find ways to share the love of the Creator with your brothers and sisters, then you have done something of great value, and accomplished a feat few upon your planet can name as their own.

It is the still pool again, in another form. Not the powers you can develop, not the experiences you can collect, but the face looking back at you, and what you decide to do with what you see there. The beginning and the end of the search, in calm, clear water.

Thank you for listening.

title: Equal at Dusk
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: equal at dusk.

Tonight Hatonn borrows a parable from the holy works, and it is one of those stories that gets more uncomfortable the longer you sit with it. It is about a vineyard, and about pay day.

The grapes are ready for harvest, and in the morning the owner hires laborers, who trudge out to earn their day's pay. But the harvest is large, so at midday he goes back to the marketplace and hires more. In the afternoon, still more. Finally, in the cool of the evening, with only a brief spell of work left, he hires the last of them. Then twilight sends its violet rays along the soft lines of the hills, and the workers gather to collect their wages.

And behold, Hatonn says, those who worked through the heat of the morning and the glare of the afternoon, those who worked only in the afternoon, and those who worked very briefly in the cool of the evening, are all paid the same.

Is this the yardstick by which you measure yourself, he asks? Do you feel you work longer or harder than others, and so deserve more? Do you find your own offerings of love and light slightly tainted, because you know you are offering them to someone who slept through the morning and wasted the afternoon, and will gain the same reward as you?

I admire how directly he names the resentment. Anyone who has tried to live a conscientious life knows that exact taint, the quiet bookkeeping of who deserves what. And the answer is uncompromising. Would you judge yourself? Would you judge others? Nay, my friends. Whatever the behavior, yours or theirs, let one thing be uppermost in your mind. We are all the Creator. The Creator is in us all, and we in the Creator.

Go, therefore, with a free and joyful heart, he says, lifting yourself up with cheer when you feel you have fallen, offering your love and light to any who may ask, be they saint or wastrel. This way lies a great realization. And then he names it. That, my friends, is compassion.

There is a second thread in the evening that belongs with the parable. Many in the group, Hatonn observes, are tempted to regard their efforts at service as money placed in a bank, drawing interest to pay for a ticket out of this illusion when the harvest comes. But the interest, he says, is not stored up. It is returned to you instantly, to further your own efforts. Have you noticed, he asks, that the first acts of service come with difficulty, after long argument with your more selfish nature, but after enough of them, the path toward service becomes your nature, an automatic orientation, without the lengthy forethought?

So do not be disheartened, he says, by the selfishness you find in yourself. It acts as a catalyst. Every effort toward service to others, however motivated, adjusts your vibration a little further toward the selfless. The morning workers and the evening workers end the day in the same place, because the work was never really about the hours.

That is the parable's sting and its mercy. No one is ahead. No one is behind. There is only the vineyard, only the twilight, only the pay that was never wages at all.

Thank you for listening.

title: The State of Harmony
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the state of harmony.

Hatonn is away tonight, called to work in the Far East against the spread of disharmony, as Latwii puts it. So it falls to Latwii to speak, and fittingly, he chooses harmony itself as his subject, that rare condition which, he notes dryly, is not frequently found upon your planet, as evidenced by the condition of your world.

His definition is worth memorizing. Harmony, he says, is that state of being in tune with the infinite Creator which is achieved by desire. A desire for unification. A desire for knowing and experiencing that fullness of being which is the Creator within.

Note the word desire. Harmony is not an accident, not a mood that descends. It is achieved, and the achievement begins with wanting it. It is unfortunate, Latwii says, that few upon your planet seek it, for it is an endeavor that includes the welfare of those around you, and most of your people are pointed in the direction of their own interests, fearing there will not be enough to go around.

The state within the individual that leads to harmony, he says, is the same state that opens the door to any growth at all. Receptivity. Openness. The desire to attain. It is far too easy, he says, to think only of personal needs and wishes and the codes we set up for judging our lives. It is far too easy to consider only what one wants for oneself, instead of how to blend one's being with another in the state of harmony.

And here is the practical heart of it. Harmony, Latwii says, is achieved with others, in cooperative effort, as individual entities blend their energies with each other. This usually entails a kind of compromise, so that each may share with the other a common position. And the first step, he says, is to give. To recognize the needs and the rights and the position of those close about you. This giving will be reciprocated, he says, for the state of giving is based on love, and that which is love is recognized by the inner being of those to whom it is given, even when it begins modestly, with the simple recognition of another person's needs.

I love that he does not ask for grand gestures. The doorway to harmony can be as small as noticing what someone near you needs. The blending begins there.

He puts the whole teaching in a single process. People in close communication join their beings closer by agreeing to accept each other as they are, and working from that beginning point in a constant balancing of the needs and ideas and beliefs of each party. Accept each other as you are. Then balance, continuously, from there.

The questions that night reached toward the large scale, toward leaders and nations and the turning of the age. And Latwii answers with an old phrase made new. The first shall be last, he says, and the last shall be first. Those who grasp the whole world and lose their souls, what have they gained? To hold tightly to the material, he says, is to build a house upon sand. And those who govern with no concern for the welfare of those they serve will find themselves, he says, at the bottom of a pit dug with their own hands.

But the new age, he says, will also bring wonders, energies sweeping across the stage of your planet, and those who are truly concerned with serving their brothers and sisters can channel those energies into creative centers. To focus in the direction of the spirit, he says, is the means by which true survival shall be attained.

So the small teaching and the large teaching are one. In a household or on a planet, harmony is achieved the same way. By desire. By giving first. By accepting the other as they are, and blending, patiently, toward something neither of you could reach alone.

Thank you for listening.

title: Out of the Rut
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: out of the rut.

Tonight's session survives only in fragments, the tape broken and partial. But the fragments hold together around a single image, and it is a good one. Your people, Hatonn says, are forever being pulled in different directions, unable to know which way to turn, stuck in a rut that has been worn deep in the road.

Not nearly so many, he says, can see that it is easier to be in the light once one has pulled oneself out of the little rut. So many do not want to try to climb in order to see, but walk on blindly in the groove.

I keep picturing it. The rut is comfortable, in its way. The walls guide you. No decisions required. Climbing out means effort, means exposure, means you might slide back. And Hatonn does not pretend otherwise. He says he can see the horror of it, the difficulty of pulling yourself up and keeping from falling back.

But then the promise. When one truly seeks the light, he says, no matter if one falls back, one may rise again stronger, with eyes that more clearly see the direction from which the light shines. The fall does not disqualify you. It trains your eyes.

The other fragment in the tape belongs with this. The unknown voice that opens the evening speaks of the dying of the year, the fall coming on, things in the natural world beginning to die or lie dormant. But these endings, the voice says, are really only starting points of new beginnings. Even as the leaves cease to be green, they are still beautiful, and still they look to the sunlight. After the bare period of fall and winter, they shall begin anew.

So the two fragments are one teaching. The rut is not a verdict. The bare season is not an ending. What looks like the stopping place is the starting place, if you are willing to climb.

We of Hatonn, the voice says, are ever ready to aid any to climb from the rut into the light. We shall be with you in your meditation, seeking with you. That is the whole of the fragment, and honestly, it is enough. A hand offered. A rut. A climb. The light, waiting at the top of it.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Flower's Service
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the flower's service.

Tonight Hatonn asks you to picture a flower. Not a poetic flower, a particular one. A flower that has decided it will not be of service. It will not accept service either. It will remain independent.

The sun shines upon the flower, he says, and before the flower can think, it opens and receives the light. Rain falls, and before it realizes, its roots have drunk and kept their health and growth. The bud opens and becomes the blossom. And before the flower has time to think, the bee has taken from it and given to it the propagation of its life. The services it has given, it has forgotten.

Listen to how he tallies it up. The flower has inadvertently been beautiful, giving each passerby a vision of perfection and radiance. It has given the bee the honey that sustains it. It has breathed into the atmosphere the very oxygen your peoples must have to survive. All without trying. All without deciding.

My friends, he says, there is no way you can refrain from accepting service and being of service. You are interlocked and meshed in the tapestry of giving and receiving, and it takes a great deal of effort to refrain from realizing all that you receive and all that you may give.

And here is the sentence I want to sit with. Among your peoples, he says, it is not uncommon to realize you are receiving gifts from others. But it is very common to refrain from the realization that you have many gifts to give, and that you are giving those gifts without effort, without trying, with your very existence.

Think about that. The service you are already performing, right now, by existing, by being who you are, in the rooms you walk through. Each of you, he says, like a flower, is beautiful and radiant and perfect. And although you may not see yourself in this light, there are those who do, who find in you an inspiration of thought and feeling that they need, though you have no consciousness of being of service.

So before you try so very hard to learn the ways of service, he says, begin here. Give thanks for the love within you that unifies you with all there is. For the beginning of service comes before you are even aware of the process. In your most selfish or secluded moment, he says, you are but pausing and learning, adding your sums wrongly and thinking again. For the essence of your life is love, and it is out of your hands. You, like the flower, will glow according to your nature, and those about you will realize the love within you, without effort, without trying, without pain.

And then the bedrock, the sentence the whole evening rests on. Lay to rest the thought that you could be trying harder, that you could be doing better, that you could be more loving. It is well to have the will to be of service, he says, but first it is well to know your nature. My friends, you are love. You are a part of the original Thought of the Creator. You are all that you seek.

Bloom as you will, he says. And remember to give thanks.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Range of Responses
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the range of responses.

Is there any love left on this planet? Hatonn opens tonight by taking the question seriously, because he knows many in the circle have asked it. There seems to be so much contention, so much strife between peoples and groups and nations. Many seek for love, he says, and seem to come away empty.

His answer begins with an observation that steadies everything after it. There is no shortage of love. What there is, is an illusion of contention lying heavy over the planet, and within that illusion, every situation you meet is a catalyst. Listen to how he defines it. A catalyst is an ingredient which of itself has no polarity, no charge. But when you interact with it, it allows you to perceive in a variety of manners.

In other words, nothing that happens to you comes pre labeled. Each situation offers a range of possible responses. At one end, he says, the concern of the individual for self. At the other end, love. Between them, everything you have ever felt. There may be strife. There may be confusion. There may be frustration. There may be momentary acceptance and lapses into anger and then acceptance again. There may be indifference. There may be a loving acceptance of the situation and of all the entities within it.

I find that list quietly liberating. All of those responses are on the same scale. None of them is a different universe from the others. You place yourself somewhere on the range with each response you choose, and the placement is never final.

And here is the sentence I keep underlining. Love, he says, does make itself available at every turn in your activities, for it is within your own being, and therefore within your own grasp. Not at some turns. At every turn. However far toward the self concern end you may have placed yourself this morning, the other end of the range has not moved.

He gives you a way to watch yourself move along it. Those who seek shall find, he says. Those who knock upon the door of love shall find that door opened, and the bounty of love pouring forth from their very being. For that door upon which you knock is within your heart of hearts. Each time you find one more ounce of love added to the scales of your response, you will find the balance tipping toward love.

An ounce. Not a transformation, not a conversion, an ounce. The scale tips the way scales tip, gradually, then all at once. That is the pace of the path, and Hatonn seems entirely at peace with it.

The questions that night ranged widely, and two answers belong in this telling. Asked about leadership, and whether a competitive role must corrupt, Hatonn refuses the premise. No role, he says, no position, implies contention or disharmony in itself. Each role offers the full range of possibilities. The heart of the experience lies within the entity. How shall love be sought? How shall love be expressed? How shall love be shared? There is no experience upon your planet, he says, that does not offer the possibility of the expression of love.

And asked about the great voids the astronomers had found, those regions of the universe seemingly empty of stars, he answers with characteristic wonder. Each area of the creation, he says, may be looked upon as a living being. Such voids may be quite advanced beings, existing in a manner we ourselves do not completely understand. That all such areas are beings, he says, is without a doubt in our way of thinking. Just what the nature of their existence is, we share your ignorance.

I love that he says that. We share your ignorance. It is the most honest sentence in the evening, and it sits naturally beside the rest. The scale, the door, the ounce of love. You do not need to understand the voids. You only need to know which end of the range you are reaching for, and to reach, one more time, today.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Foolishness of Love
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the foolishness of love.

Much of tonight's session is given over to exercising new instruments, voice after voice attempting to speak Hatonn's thoughts for the first time, hesitating, doubting, trying again. And out of that halting practice comes the teaching of the evening, which is about the price of admission.

The opening as a channel, Hatonn says, is both quite simple and quite difficult. It is simple for those who are willing to appear quite foolish, and to allow our thoughts to be spoken by their own voices as they appear within their minds. It is quite difficult, he says, for those who would wish to maintain a certainty that they shall not appear foolish.

Every new instrument, he explains, goes through the same doubt. The thoughts perceived in the mind seem like the instrument's own manufacture. Are these really Hatonn's words, or am I making this up as I go? And his answer is gentle and absolute. The contact is real, he says, and the doubt will dilute with practice, again and again, within the group.

But then he widens the frame, and the teaching stops being about channeling at all. Upon your planet at this time, he says, it is the experience of any who seek to love that this experience shall render one quite familiar with the feelings of foolishness. For upon your planet it is quite foolish, it would seem, to love without the expectation of return. To give for no reason other than to give, to one who needs. That, he says, looks like foolishness to the world.

I keep turning that over. The willingness to seem foolish is not a side effect of the spiritual life. It is the doorway. The channel must risk sounding foolish to speak. The lover must risk looking foolish to love. The world keeps score, and both of them fail the world's test on purpose.

And Hatonn gives the reason it is safe to take the risk. What we transmit through your instrument, he says, is none other than the love and the light of the one infinite Creator which exists within your very being. It is not something alien to you. It is what you are most intimately acquainted with, when you open your being to the love that resides within.

The questions that night touched on a man who had lived this teaching in public. Asked about the one known as Sadat, Hatonn speaks of a man unafraid to do the things that flowed within and throughout him, isolated by choice from many of his own countrymen, doing what his inner light required in a region where fear kept most people from expressing their feelings. His mourning, Hatonn says, was far greater than what the cameras showed, for many had to suppress their grief out of fear. But his example remains, of what one can accomplish by doing that which flows within, manifested in physical action.

One need not affect many, Hatonn adds. As one shines, one is seen, and by flowing within oneself, one touches others, whether one actively seeks to do so or not. For we all are love and light, and the flowing of love and light touches all those around those who become aware.

So the evening ends where the new channels began, with the risk and the reward held together. Speak, though you may sound foolish. Love, though you may look foolish. What comes through you was never foreign to you. It was yours all along, waiting for someone willing to look a little foolish to let it out.

Thank you for listening.

title: Say What Comes
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: say what comes.

Laitos is a teacher of a very particular kind. While others in the archive teach love and philosophy, Laitos teaches people how to listen. These evenings are training sessions, and the instruments are new, nervous, unsure whether the thoughts in their minds are their own or someone else's. And the first thing Laitos tells them is almost too simple to believe.

Desire is the key to the contact. That is the whole teaching in one line, and Laitos repeats it in different ways all evening. You do not need some great depth of trance. You do not need to be special. You need only desire the contact, and it will be given. The greater the desire, the more fully the work can be done with you.

But there is a trap, and it catches everyone. The new instrument receives a thought and instantly asks, was that me or was that them? Laitos is gentle about this. Analysis is natural, he says. But it is also the single greatest obstacle to the contact. His advice is disarmingly plain. Do not try to discriminate between their thoughts and your own. Just say what is available for the saying.

I love that line. It dissolves the whole problem. Because in the end, he says, you will discover that all sources are one. The information is the Creator's information, whether it arrives through your own mind or through theirs. The greater the desire, the more the understanding. The point is not to be right about the source. The point is to let it flow.

Someone asks how to be sure contact has really been made. Laitos answers with something I think about often. We do not deal in certainty, he says, for this is a phenomenon which has no proof. Proof, he adds, would be the greatest infringement upon your free will. If you want a sign, you can ask for one beforehand, a physical sensation that tells you the contact is beginning. But even that, you can talk yourself out of.

Another asks why the contact keeps slipping away. Was it a bad contact? Was it anxiety? Laitos confirms it plainly. Anxiety is like static on a radio. The mind must be cleared and relaxed, not deepened. It is the clearing of the mind that matters, not the depth of the trance. Take deep breaths, he says, and simply speak the thoughts as they are perceived, without analysis or doubt.

And underneath all the instruction there is a tenderness that runs through the whole evening. Every new instrument is thanked by name. Every effort is honored. Laitos promises to be with each of them in their private meditations, whenever a simple request is made. The relationship, he makes clear, is not a technique but a friendship.

So the lesson of this session is really a lesson about listening itself. Clear the mind. Drop the analysis. Speak what comes. And trust that the desire that brought you to the practice is already the contact you are looking for.

Thank you for listening.

title: Love That Endures
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: love that endures.

Hatonn begins with a line I have never quite recovered from. He wants to talk about an aspect of love that is seldom understood among our peoples, and that is endurance. Not passion, not devotion, but endurance. Staying. Going on. Love as the thing that does not quit.

Your life, he says, is made of peaks and valleys. On the peaks you feel invincible. You stand in the euphoria of the heights and you are sure you can carry it through anything that comes. But this, he says, is not so. There is no mountain high enough to bridge the valleys. And the valleys come. The difficult and dreary times. The stretches when it seems impossible to find a positive reason for your existence.

And yet, he goes on, there is no valley deep enough to keep you from scaling the next height. Listen to how he puts it. How easy it is, he says, to love and to be loved upon the peaks of your life. How easy to express the graceful phrase, the caring thought, the heartfelt deed. And when you have once again walked into the vale and are locked in the cage of sorrow, how then can you reach through the bars and offer up love?

You cannot, he admits, not easily. In the valley you are a prisoner of your sorrow and you do not know how to do these things. But then comes the turn that makes this more than comfort. If you experience the alternation of joy and sorrow to a great enough extent, with enough clarity of perception, you may discover in this very cycle one enduring thing. And that, he says, is yourself.

Your mind makes peaks and rejoices in freedom. Your mind makes valleys and imprisons itself in sorrow. But your mind is always your mind. Your consciousness, your beingness, never changes, never alters, and does indeed endure. And you are part of an original Thought, part of what he calls love. As long as your consciousness endures, so shall love.

Love is not a property of the heights of joy, he says. Nor are you bereft of it in the utmost depths of despair. For you are love. It is always with you, no matter how distorted your perception of yourself, no matter how separated you feel from the warmth and safety of love. You cannot deny your being. You cannot escape your nature.

So from time to time, he suggests, imagine yourself as the watcher of a picture that moves upon a screen. That picture is yourself as you act from day to day, moved by the winds of experience. And you, the watcher, see something deeper than the folly and the failures. The watcher sees the reality behind all of it. The watcher sees love.

Every moment you face, pleasant or troubling, is an opportunity to examine and feel, a chance to grow. A lesson unlearned repeats itself. But the one who watches, the one who endures, is learning it even now, one valley at a time.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Old Man on the Shore
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the old man on the shore.

Tonight Hatonn tells a story. It begins with a small child abandoned on a sea coast, forced to survive on his own meager knowledge. He wanders the shore for years, the crashing waves almost speaking to him, yet never quite. One day he stumbles upon an old man sitting on the beach, gazing sightlessly toward the horizon. The boy sits beside him and listens. He grows drowsy. He begins to dream. And he begins to understand.

He realizes the old man is himself. The ocean is himself. All who went before, all he has tried to rediscover, are himself. The boy awakens. The old man is gone, and yet the teacher, the sharer, is still there, for he was himself.

I have read this story many times and it still stops me. Hatonn tells it to underline the importance of what you do. The acts you perform, the efforts you make toward growth and understanding and the assistance of others, are all acts of service, for as you learn for yourself, you learn for all. For all are yourself.

Do not be ashamed, then, he says, if your heart directs you in paths of learning as well as paths of service. To understand the mysteries of your universe is to love it. And to love a part is to love the all.

Then he offers a second image, and this one is water. You are a drop of water, he says, and the path you walk is the path of that drop toward the infinite sea of creation. A drop may seem powerless. You may feel lacking or limited. But water is continuous and is not separated from itself. It falls in drops in service to the fruits of the earth, and yet as it gathers and moves toward the great oceans, does it not carve mighty channels that men could not hew with all their might?

Water is quiet, he says, and yet when stirred can be the mightiest of avengers, changing physical landscapes in minutes. In your meditations, then, take each limitation and each disappointment and offer them up as drops of water. See them dissolve in a pure, clear ocean of the infinite Creator. Then let the rainbow of sunlight through that water fill your heart and send you forth to serve.

You are serving yourself, he says, for all that you meet and all that you seek is yourself. If you love the ocean of the Creator, then you will learn to love each drop of water, each apparently individualized portion of that ocean. Yourself and all others. All circumstances and all times.

Even your faith has its seasons. There will be times when your search seems to wither, when all feels dying and without meaning. But if you are patient, you will feel the rain nourishing you again. You will feel the love and the light that are you, and you will grow, blossom, and be renewed.

Thank you for listening.

title: Know Trouble as Friend
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: know trouble as friend.

Tonight begins with a story about a young violinist, a prodigy whose gift flowed from her without effort. She had never had to work. And then one day, before a concert, she learns the orchestra has rehearsed a different piece, one she does not know. She has only hours. The unfamiliar score stares at her like an enemy. She works feverishly, desperately, and cannot play it through once without errors.

She takes her bows before the full house. The music is jumbled in her head. And she plays as she has never played before. Notes are missed, but they go by so quickly the reviewers miss them, for the piece is played with passion and with feeling. And she goes away knowing, for the first time, the experience of joy in her chosen art.

There are many times, Hatonn says, when things flow easily and you accept your gifts thoughtlessly, for they are not hard won. Then a whirlwind seems to hit you. A dilemma, a difficulty, an argument. And you wonder why you must go through it. It is your chance, he says, for growth. In the situation where you are tried and tested, you are given a great opportunity, and your response, no matter how flawed, will bring you joy if it contains the best you can give.

How easy it is to be pleasant when there is no reason not to be. Use the calm times, he says, in meditation, in appreciation of what you so easily take for granted. And when the whirlwind takes you, realize this is most appropriate for those experiencing your density. This is the way the work is done.

And then he says the line that gives this evening its title. Know trouble as your friend. All things and all qualities are of the one Creator, whose only wish for each is love. The ways of this love are many and varied, but all ways are love. All difficulties lead to calm, to light, to beauty.

Love, he says, is far beyond what you think of as love. Its characteristics include those of the whirlwind, ceaselessly beating against your life to aid you as you wish to be aided, to change you as you choose to change. The whirlwind is of the Creator, and it will place you safe once again in that quiet cove of calm, where you may again seek in meditation to understand, and seek in the giving of yourself to express that understanding of love.

All the false images of your illusion lead to the one original Thought, which is the truth you seek. The whirlwind does not destroy you. It delivers you.

Thank you for listening.

title: Children of Light
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: children of light.

Tonight's teaching comes at the close of a long training session, and it is about identity. Hatonn says you are strangers in a strange land, dealing with many foolish and petty occasions, and that in this confusing density it is a difficult thing to remember who you are.

But there is, he says, a master, and you are his children. And the mark within you, as his children, is that you are children of light. The light within you marks you as the Creator's own. And then he says something I want you to hear slowly. No circumstance, no thought, no behavior, no error, no difficulty, no limitation can remove this mark from your very being. You rest in the arms of the Creator. There is no moment in eternity when this is not so.

The illusion is strong, he admits, and often dark. But there is a light within you and you are the Creator's own. You shall never be forgotten. You shall never be lost. As you seek, that light intensifies, and as it brightens, you begin to light the way for others.

Others will tell you about your light, he says, for many cannot see it themselves. Trust no words, no thoughts, no behavior in yourself or others, but be grounded in the knowledge of your birthright, of your identity in the light. Call upon it. Speak to it. And never fear that you shall be lost from it.

Do not attempt to ask yourself to believe anything, he says. You are what you are. That is enough. Seek then to know who and what you are. In your meditation, in your seeking, in your crying and in your laughter, call upon us and we are with you. For we are all children of one Creator and are indeed one being.

Laitos, who shares the evening, adds a quieter image. Your lessons, he says, are as leaves in autumn. They accumulate and must be dealt with. You may push them aside or ignore them, but they are there, and within them is the potential for growth. If you break them down and examine them, as you would mulch the leaves, they will aid your growth as the mulch aids the soil.

So the message of the night is really one thing said two ways. Nothing you do can unmake what you are. And nothing you face is without its use. The light is the given. The lessons are the mulch. Both are yours.

Thank you for listening.

title: Love Greater Than Judgment
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: love greater than judgment.

Hatonn's subject tonight is openness, and he begins it plainly. There is an aspect of love that lets you remain open to everything around you without judging and without hiding. And as you grow in awareness, he warns, there is a temptation that comes with it. The more you see, the more you judge. And judging, he says, is like taking steps backward along the path you have begun to travel.

For all within this illusion are part of the One, and no one is worse or better than any other. By remaining open to the people and events around you, you can benefit from the lesson each one offers, if you will accept it simply as a lesson to be felt and learned.

Then he tells a small story. A man is convinced the end of the world is coming, and he goes about begging everyone to change their ways, to be ready for the day of judgment. One pleasant sunny day, quite unexpectedly, his heart fails and he is struck down. And as he lies there he understands. His latter days have come. All that he said to others, he had in many ways forgotten to apply to himself. It was he who was under judgment. He had judged himself and found himself wanting.

To refrain from discrimination is not wise, Hatonn is careful to add. You were given a tool, and that tool is your intellect, and within it the powers of discrimination and judgment, and when used correctly much may be done with them. But love, he says, is greater than judgment and wiser. For it knows that no matter what you see, you see yourself. No matter what you think about another, you think it of yourself.

I keep coming back to that line. It does not forbid judgment. It simply outranks it. Love is the larger frame, and in that frame, every condition and situation, every seeming error of the heart and mind and spirit, leads ever onward to a final, complete dissolution in love.

He closes with a thought I want to carry with you. His message is to the heart, he says, not to the mind. Within you lies the universe. That which you see with your physical eyes is but an image of that which you contain. To share love, he says, is the greatest privilege of which we know.

Thank you for listening.

title: What Desire Tunes
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: what desire tunes.

This is a fragment of an evening, pieces of tape with gaps in them, and yet the teaching that survives is whole. Hatonn is answering a question about meditation, and what he says reframes the practice entirely. In the meditative state, he says, all is possible. And the tuning of that state is accomplished through desire.

Your desire, whatever it might be, may be more easily manifest in the state of meditation, for in that state you are reaffirming your connection with the one Creator. You are retracing, he says, the steps you have made from your conscious self back toward your source. As you retrace them, you find opening before you any avenue which you seek. So it is your desire that tunes the state of meditation, and it is your desire that determines how you use it.

There is a beautiful honesty in this. Meditation is not a blank emptying of yourself. It is a directed thing, and the direction comes from what you want most deeply. That is why the practice matters more than the posture, and the longing matters more than the technique.

Earlier in the evening Hatonn says something else that has stayed with me. When you serve as an instrument, as a channel for the Creator, you are trying to condense the beingness of the Creator into words. And words, he says, distort. There are no words which can fully express the beingness of the one Creator that resides within you. Every message is a crystallization, and every crystallization is a small distortion. The truth is larger than the language that carries it.

Someone asks whether meditation can help recall previous lives. Hatonn says it can, but that it is difficult, for in meditation you deactivate the conscious mind, and you need some part of that mind to serve as a guide through the subconscious, like a guide leading a journey through unfamiliar country. Possible, he says, but not easy. The meditative state is better suited to what it does best, which is to retrace your steps toward the Creator.

So the evening leaves us with one clear instruction. Follow your desire into the silence. Let it tune you. And know that the words you bring back will always be a little smaller than the country you visited.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Healer Within
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the healer within.

Tonight Hatonn speaks of healing, and his first sentence changes everything about the subject. Healing, he says, is a function of the one to be healed desiring to be healed. No one else can do it for you. Others may serve as a catalyst, but in the final analysis, the healing is done by the one to be healed, and it is the Creator, residing within that one, who does the healing.

For those who wish to aid another, he offers a method. In meditation, image the one to be healed in as much detail as you can, seeing the condition that needs healing. Then replace that image with another. See the same one in the healed condition, surrounded by love and light, every part glowing. Hold each image for some minutes. Then release the images, so that higher forces, as he puts it, might take them over and fill in the flesh on the bone of your image.

And then he turns to anger, and gives one of the most practical meditations in the archive. If you feel anger toward another, he says, go into the meditative state and see that entity receiving your anger. See the effect of it upon them. Then see that entity as yourself. See yourself as the one receiving the anger you have generated. Feel its effects within your own being. Carry it to its logical conclusion in your mind. Let the image remain until the anger has been spent and felt in full.

Then, for a moment, image its opposite. Let that image disappear like a small beacon, and approach it by a process of natural discovery. See the other still as both the other and yourself. Make no attempt to guide yourself toward anger or toward love. Let your being proceed on its own, until you feel the love you imaged momentarily begin to fill your being, which is also the being of the other.

And then see both emotions, the anger and the love, in your mind as imbalance. See the imbalance of anger, but see the balance of anger and love. Then accept yourself and forgive yourself, and see yourself as whole and complete, as is the Creator, which you are. See yourself experiencing both emotions as means by which the Creator might know itself.

It is a remarkable sequence. Not repression. Not indulgence. Discovery. And it ends where all of his teaching ends, in the recognition that the one you were angry at was never separate from you at all.

Thank you for listening.

title: You Already Are
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: you already are.

The season is turning toward Christmas, and Hatonn speaks to the loneliness that can gather inside the celebration. Many reach out and touch one another at this time of year, he says, but there are those who build walls between themselves and the love that is so strong then. They do not realize that they are love and light. They need only open themselves a small bit, and they may see it.

And then he asks the question that carries the whole evening. What is it, he says, that constitutes yourself? Feel your body, your feet, your hands. Is that where you are? Perhaps not. Look in your mind, in your thinking. Am I speaking to you, to the essence of yourself? Not yet, he says, have we found each other. For that which is you is closer to you than your body, more nigh to you than your thoughts, dearer and surer than your breath, and just as difficult to recognize.

In this illusion it is very difficult to know even your self, and it is only in knowing the self that you can know another, that you can share with another, that you can rejoice and laugh and give. Is it any wonder, he asks, that so many are alone at the very time their culture urges them to rejoice? The urge from without to pretend to be happy is itself what causes the loneliness.

So he gives the instruction simply. As you enter this season, seek to know your own self. Find that love which is your true being, for in knowing that one simple spark which is of the one Creator, you will know every person you meet, and there can be no division between you. Then you may truly share the love of the Creator, and let its light come forth from your eyes.

There is nothing you need do, he says, for you already are what you seek. If you want a basic method, as always, he suggests meditation, meditation and meditation. The attempt, the persistence and the desire are essential. Your estimate of your success is inessential.

That last line is worth keeping. It is not your measurement of the meditation that matters. It is the attempt. Keep attempting, and what you seek will find you already there, because you never left.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Child Who Flew
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the child who flew.

Tonight Hatonn tells a story that sounds like a fairy tale until it doesn't. A child is born, normal in every way, except that he is aware of the world around him. He has not been indoctrinated into disbelieving his own perception. He simply knows the substance of which his world is composed, and the malleability of his surroundings, and his ability to flow with them as a feather flows on a stream.

The children accept him easily. The elders do not. They find their own distorted explanations for what he can do, and when the child begins to fly, they declare him evil and put him on trial. He is condemned to death. His physical body is terminated. But the child, unaware that death is supposed to be frightening, simply continues to fly.

The child in all of us continues to fly, Hatonn says. We can load it down with the heavy burdens of our supposed knowledge and wisdom. We can crush ourselves to the earth with our needs, our possessions, the heavy burdens we create for ourselves. Or we can see them in their proper perspective, as malleable conditions we created for the purpose of our own learning, and relinquish them when we are finished.

And then he says it plainly. My brothers, my sisters, if your burdens are heavy, lay them down and come fly.

He adds that there is a gap between the inspiration and the practice. He has not forgotten the gravity that holds you down, both physically and metaphysically. And he suggests you lay aside your metaphysical gravity and take your birthright as a co-creator of this infinite universe.

True flight, he says, is not mechanical. The true self is revealed to the self unexpectedly, as if you walked into a strange room and caught sight of your face in the mirror. Within the bleak outline of difficult days, or the rich outline of good ones, something unexpected occurs, and a discovery is made. These things cannot be predicted or planned. They are the revelations of the self to the self.

That true self, he says, is love. And its nature is such that it opens to you, in all unity, all of creation. Here is true flight. Here is the capacity to be the essence, to experience all that there is. Your spirit can fly. Come fly with us, he says, in a universe filled with the love and the light of the infinite Creator.

Thank you for listening.

title: You Do Not Seek in Vain
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: you do not seek in vain.

Laitos greets the group with something rare in the archive, a mystery stated plainly. You are in the minority among your peoples, he says. You seek the invisible, and you do not find the visible satisfactory or sufficient. You seek the idea, and you do not find practicality a reasonable excuse. You seek service, and you do not accept that being self-sufficient is service enough.

And we are with you, he says, to share with you a mystery. That mystery is that you do not seek in vain. That mystery is the mystery of an infinite creation, of an original Thought that has created all that there is, including an infinite array of things that cannot be seen with the physical eye, cannot be touched, cannot be experienced, until one thing occurs, until one door is opened. And that one thing is the seeking you are now engaged in.

I want to sit with that for a moment, because it reverses the usual bargain. The seeking is not the price you pay to reach the door. The seeking is the door opening. The moment you turn toward the invisible, the invisible has already begun to turn toward you.

Laitos is mostly a trainer of instruments, and much of the evening is spent working with new channels, patiently, name by name. But he pauses for a question about healing, and his answer carries the same teaching. Your desire to be healed, he says, is itself the greatest aid to your healing, for your desire pierces the protective shell that holds your physical vehicle in its configuration, and allows the healing energy that many send you to enter.

The visualization he recommends is simple. See your body surrounded by light, the healing love and light of the one Creator, entering through your lower energy centers and your feet, circulating through your body, gathering where healing is most needed. And then see yourself completely healthy and healed. The desire opens the shell. The light does the rest.

He closes the evening as he opened it, with gratitude for the calling. We treasure each experience, he says, and thank each present for adding another voice to the call of service. The minority that seeks the invisible is not alone in it. It is being met, evening by evening, thought by thought, by those who seek the same light from the other side.

Thank you for listening.

title: Exiles of the Soul
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: exiles of the soul.

The voice that carries this evening belongs to Oxal, and the message is for anyone who has ever felt like a stranger in the world they live in. You, my friends, are in exile, he says. All upon your planet are in a strange land. There is no comfort for the spirit in the spirit of your culture. The planet that man has made is a strange and barbarous territory.

You are in exile in your bodies. There is within you a knowledge, a remembrance, a memory of the light and the infinite life of your true existence and of your true body. But here you are, cast away. And what have you done, you exiles of the soul? Have you banded together defensively against the pain of living? Have you attempted to convince yourselves that exile is home? Examine your actions and your thoughts, he says, and you may find in yourself many traces of the behavior of a stranger in a strange land.

It is a startling diagnosis, and it lands because it is true. We do arrange our lives as if the exile were the home. We defend, we accumulate, we pretend to be at ease in a territory our spirits never chose.

But Oxal does not leave you there. There is comfort, he says. There is complete and utter comfort. It is in looking outward that you miss the one source of home, for to find that home you must look within the self. Beneath all that you have been taught, beneath all that you have rationalized, there lies a homeland and a true being, so deeply fixed within you that you cannot lose it and you cannot forget it. It is not to be earned, he says. It may only be sought.

Seek, then, the peace of your true home, the balm of your true identity. And in that knowledge, look out upon this illusion and see it in love and in light. If you seek wisdom, you shall not find it in your illusion. In meditation, go home. For that home is yours by right of infinite birth.

Let there be no division in yourself, he says. Cease all confusion and know that exiles think strange things. Seek that which awaits within. The homeland is not a place you travel to. It is the place you never left.

Thank you for listening.

title: Room for the Eagle
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: room for the eagle.

This is a short session, mostly devoted to training new instruments, but it opens with an image I cannot let go of. Laitos describes a winter scene. How high the snow is in the winter. How blue the cerulean sky. One lone eagle stalks far above, watching. His mate watches. The air is crisp, the day is long. The eagle is patient. There is a rush, a sudden emptiness where once the eagle soared. The eagle has found its food.

The beauty of the sky, the whiteness of the mountain, the crispness of the air do not disturb the hunter, Laitos says, for its seeking is quite specific. In this fair creation of the infinite Creator which you call Earth there are not only difficulties but many pleasant distractions, many lovely things. Find then within your being room for the eagle that seeks, keen-eyed and patient, for the bread of heaven.

Those things which will aid you, he says, will not come to you in a moment, until that moment comes. Keep awake.

It is a strange and wonderful instruction. The seeking is not frantic. It is not anxious. It is the patience of the eagle, high and still, watching, ready. The bread of heaven does not come on your schedule. It comes when the moment comes. Your work is only to keep the room open and stay awake.

One of the new instruments, speaking Laitos's words that evening, adds a line that belongs here. The completion of your quests, she says, will be experienced as the acceptance of yourselves, as all is accepted. The length of the journey is limited only by each individual's free will.

So the eagle and the journey meet in the same teaching. Seek with patience. Accept yourself. And stay awake for the moment when what you seek is suddenly, simply, there.

Notice too that the eagle does not chase the sky. It does not worry about the loveliness around it or hurry the hunt. Its seeking is specific, and that specificity is what makes it patient. We might borrow some of that in our own seeking, instead of scattering our attention across every pleasant distraction and calling it growth.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Bubblegum Wrapper
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the bubblegum wrapper.

Tonight is mostly a working session, the training of new instruments, but the questions at the end carry the teaching. Someone asks whether, as new questions arise about the energy centers of the body, the group can keep bringing them to Hatonn for clarity. And Hatonn says yes, with a condition that has stayed with me.

Each entity, he says, must keep foremost in mind the need for renewed seeking, for never resting upon any information, whether it be of great inspirational nature or simply that found upon, as he puts it, your bubblegum wrapper.

I love that he will not let even his own messages be exempt. No teaching, however inspired, is a place to stop. The seeking must renew itself constantly, or it becomes another kind of sleep.

Another asks about a troubling sending, an opposition felt during meditation, and wonders how it could get through the group's protective work. Hatonn answers carefully. Each entity in seeking the Creator will meet what appears to be an opposition, a separative factor. And each must determine that this seeming opposition is a part of the great Self, and as part of that great Self, must be treated with the greatest love, care and consideration.

Do not fight the shadow, in other words. Recognize it. Love it. It is part of the same Self you are seeking.

And the evening ends with Nona, who prefers not to speak, offering only their vibration to all those who seek to heal. Sometimes the teaching is words. Sometimes, as Nona reminds us, the teaching is simply the presence, the vibration, the willingness to be there.

There is mercy in this teaching too. Never resting on any information does not mean never trusting anything. It means holding even your most cherished insights the way you would hold a bird in your hand, lightly enough that it can still fly. The moment a truth becomes a wall you lean on, Hatonn is saying, it has stopped being a truth for you and become a resting place. And the seeker is not meant to rest.

Keep seeking, keep questioning, and never mistake any single answer for the end of the road.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Trackless Desert
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the trackless desert.

It is the Christmas season, and Hatonn looks at the crowded world and names what he sees. Your streets are crowded, he says. Crowded parking lots, crowded schedules, many concerns. Your people seem to have a great overdose, as he puts it, of civilization. To the simple joys of a season in which the trees are bare and the roots rest deep, so much has been added that it is almost gaudier than the bright colors of June.

Are the thoughts with which you fill your minds, he asks, as beautiful as flowers, as sweet smelling as the evergreen trees you use to celebrate this season? It is easy, he says, to lose yourself in the crowded maze of your civilization. And he asks you to remember that this is also the season when the trees are bare, when all has gone to seed and lies quiet in the ground, when the surface of things does not really matter.

In the world of the Creator, he says, this is the season for true birth, for true nurture, and for that great focused silence which brings new growth. He reminds you that in the holy work you call the Bible, the life of the one known as Jesus is full of times spent alone. Perhaps you cannot find a wilderness in these crowded days. But consider the virtue of finding that silence within yourself, in which you cease to follow the road of everyday life and find yourself upon the trackless desert, where nothing is previously set or known.

Allow yourself to listen within yourself, he says. There is a source of love which can only speak to one who asks. The content of that speaking cannot be predicted, but there are qualities that can certainly be shared, clarity and sweetness. Do not expect the road to be already drawn for you, for the wilderness is trackless. And yet, from each meditation, the way before you becomes less crowded, the road more wide, and the possibilities for love more evident.

Take these words, he says, not as infallible, but only as words from a friend, from a brother, from yourself, for are we not one? And as the crowded season presses in, look up into the limitless sky, and know that there is no true reason to feel anything but love.

Thank you for listening.

title: Love, Given Freely
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: love, given freely.

Tonight's teaching comes from Latwii, answering a question about the pain of emotional relationships, and it contains the clearest definition of love in the archive. Listen to it in his words first. The concept of love, he says, is the free giving of the self without reservation to another, because the other is as it is.

The giving of love which demands that another be other than it is, he says, is a distortion of love, and it has severe ramifications. It results in emotional pain and the withdrawal of love. And then the entity that has been hurt feels an aversion to further love, because love has never been experienced in a positive way.

He names what has gone wrong in our relationships with a phrase that stings. In our society, he says, there is a bartering of emotions. Love has been colored and twisted by our peoples for many generations, until it is misapprehended as something that can be divided into parts and traded as a commodity. We keep the scales balanced. We give so much and expect so much back. And this bartering, he says, hinders the free flow of what little love we know.

But the pure experiencing of love, he says, is the giving with no expectation of return. And even though the one who loves in this way might be viewed as most foolish, it is such foolishness which shall eventually be seen to be the container which knows no limits, and can therefore contain the concept of love.

And then he says something that completes the teaching. Where there is love freely given for no reason and with no expectation of return, there is created within the entity who gives it a vacuum, which shall draw unto that entity that which it gives. For there is nothing truly apart from an entity, for all beings are one. When one is loved, for any reason or no reason, then all are loved, and the self also finds its love.

Give freely, and the giving returns to you. Not as a transaction, but as the nature of things. That is the whole economy of love in a single image, a vacuum that fills itself.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Lonely Pilgrimage
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the lonely pilgrimage.

The journey you are on, Hatonn says, will bring periods in which you feel your pilgrimage is no longer functioning properly. To speak to this, he tells a small story. A young man sets out alone to make a journey, and as he seeks, he changes. He grows older year by year. He visits homes that seem so normal and so pleasant, and he asks himself why, if he is like other men, he cannot have such pleasantness.

Still he seeks. Still he sheds what light he has upon those he meets. And one day he meets an old woman. She is alone but has not always been so. Her face is wrinkled, but her eyes sparkle. The man, no longer so young, asks her why the seeker must always have such a lonely pilgrimage. The old woman smiles gently. There are no rules to a pilgrimage, she says, except those that you make for yourself. Examine that which you think you need. If it stays the same, there is not the beginning of the opportunity for growth.

Why, the young man says, you were married for many, many years. Ah, yes, says the old woman. But we were both pilgrims.

That last line undoes the whole question. The loneliness was never in the circumstance. Two people can walk the same road together and both be pilgrims. The solitude the seeker fears is not cured by company or by solitude. It is cured by seeing the journey for what it is.

For the dead spots on the road, Hatonn suggests the balm of meditation, while remembering that it was your choice to begin this pilgrimage. Take yourself into yourself, he says, for in meditation the conscious and the unconscious meet, become acquainted, and begin to merge into one ever larger beacon of light.

And he ends with a promise I want you to carry. Pilgrims are happy, he says, as no other entities can ever be, when they are changing. In any crucible of transformation, joy is an inevitable byproduct.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Two Directions
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the two directions.

This is a fragment of an evening, only a few minutes of tape, but the teaching is complete. With change, Hatonn says, there are two directions a person can face. One may look forward, or one may look back toward the direction from which one has come. Both, he says, are equally valuable, although it is easy to be caught in focusing on only one.

One of the great uses of meditation, he says, is the stabilizing of these two views. You look upon the past deeds of your life and the experiences that brought you where you are today, and you look ahead to the new, as yet unrealized goal that each of us carries. And that goal, he says, can be guided by the will of each individual along the journey.

We all carry pictures in the backs of our minds, he says, specific goals, things we would like to do, things we think will help us get where we desire to be. Many of these are glimmers of possible realities. Many are modified recollections of past experiences. And among those who acknowledge they are on similar paths, there are obstacles, memories of seeds which have not come to fruit.

And it is sometimes difficult to see, he says, that there are still many more seeds which need to be planted and cultivated, to ensure further spiritual growth, individually and as a small collective of light beings desiring to be of service on the planet.

I love the image of the unplanted seeds. The past holds the seeds that did not fruit, and the future holds the seeds not yet planted, and meditation is the still point where you can look honestly in both directions at once. Not to regret the one, and not to grasp at the other, but to be stabilized between them, guided by your own will.

A short teaching, but a steady one. Look back with honesty. Look forward with intention. And plant what still needs planting. The field is yours, and the seasons are yours, and the work is only to keep turning toward it.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Practice of Being
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the practice of being.

Tonight Hatonn speaks to the seeker who is always falling short of the spiritual mark. He knows the feeling. Each in this group, he says, considers himself to fall far short. And he answers it not with a standard to meet, but with the standard dissolved.

You are not on the path only when you meditate, he says. There is no action or thought that cannot be considered in relation to the path. Do not cut any part of your life off from it. For in all stations of life, in all moods of man, there lies perfection, love, and a wonderful surety of step that only come to the mind of one who has begun the practice of being.

The instrument herself protests, in her own mind, that she is too rowdy, too often in bad humor. How can she be on the path? And Hatonn answers her, and all of us, with the question that ends the argument. How can you not be on the path? There is only one I AM, and all of you are part of it. In laughter and in tears, never fear that you have stumbled.

It is the seeking, he says, that concentrates, preserves and enlightens the organism of your spiritual self. Not the attainment. The seeking. You are as those who search through days and nights, through clarity and haze, looking restlessly for the inspiration that will be food for your true self. And the greatest adventure, he says, is not out in the world at all. It lies in the microscopic interplay within your own consciousness. Your greatest explorer could not discover any territory so vast and so uncharted as the country within you.

You are not creatures of your body, he says. You are not bound by time or space. Your birthright is what you have called Christ-consciousness. You are love. The universe is one thing. It is within you both to find that one thing and to be that one thing.

So the practice is not a posture or an hour of the day. It is the whole of your life, undivided. The rowdy days and the quiet days. The laughter and the tears. None of it is off the path, because the path is everywhere you are.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Unsoiled Garment
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the unsoiled garment.

Tonight Hatonn speaks of work, and of the strange distance our culture has put between our daily labor and our love. It was intended, he says, that you might experience your work as a form of meditation and as an experience of love. It has been many centuries since many of your peoples could profoundly experience the combination of work and love.

It has been said, to work is to pray. And for those lucky enough to have found occupations that feed the spirit as well as supply the necessities of survival, this is in the deepest sense true. But for so many, the connection between the daily life and love, between action and meditation, is not apparent. And to link them, he says, begin with the meditation rather than with the work.

Then he gives you a meditation, and it is one of the most beautiful in the archive. Imagine moving in consciousness up a great hillside, whose base is vanity, pollution, pettiness and distraction. In your spirit's garment you climb, and you can feel that garment soiled from all that touches you. So you remove the garment and cleanse yourself in the waters of a waterfall falling down the hillside, brilliant and iridescent as it sprays the rocks, the moss and the grass.

Leaning into the water, you begin to see the purity of your true being. You take up a fresh garment, a new washed linen, and you move onward until you sit at the top of the hillside. The air is warm and redolent with wild flowers, pinks and roses and whites in profusion. And as you settle into meditation, this is your consciousness. This is who you are. All of creation breathes with you and desires to be of service to you, and you in turn offer up the rhythms of your body, your mind and your spirit in service to this beautiful place.

Yes, he says, you come down again into the marketplace, where you live the illusion, where your lessons gather. But you bring with you an unsoiled garment, a cleanliness of soul, and a new vision that begins to see the top of the hillside beneath the soiled garment of all labor, all conditions, all relationships.

Within yourselves, he says, you must find a place in which, in silence, you find the creation offered unto you, and you offer yourself unto the creation. And never be discouraged if you fail to manifest what you have learned in meditation, for this is the work of your life, to find who you are. That is, to find the Creator, that one great original Thought which is love.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Ordinary Child
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the ordinary child.

On the seventh of February, in nineteen eighty-two, a Sunday evening circle gathered in meditation, and the one who calls himself Hatonn began with a story. Not a story about a hero. A story about a child nobody would have noticed.

The child, Hatonn says, was born to poor parents in a small village. He grew up, found a wife, raised his own children, grew old, and died. Nothing outstanding about him, physically or mentally. An ordinary life from beginning to end. And yet, Hatonn says, in that brief lifespan the child accomplished exactly what he had set out to do before he was born. He learned the lesson he had prescribed for himself. He did not gain great wisdom. He did not even sort out the great choice between serving himself and serving others. But he did the thing he came to do.

I love how much rests in that little story. Because most lives, when you look at them from the outside, look exactly like that one. Small. Uneventful. And Hatonn insists that the size of the life is not the measure of the learning. The lessons toward which we strive still lie far in the future for many, he says, and then he gives us the line that holds the whole evening together. One must learn to crawl, he says, before one may run.

Which brings him to the real point, and it is a tender one. There are many in your world today, he says, who are like this child. The things you seek, the revelations you hold so dear, have not been revealed to them. It is often hard to extend your love to them. Their confusion can seem almost like another species to you, a duller, dimmer one, distantly related to your own. And here Hatonn is firm and gentle at once. They are not merely your own species, he says. These are your own selves. Their lessons are as important to them as yours are to you, and their learning is paid for with as many tears and as much pain.

Loving them is not always easy, he admits, and it is sometimes poorly rewarded. But then he asks the question that stops you short. Is reward what you seek?

There is a second story tucked into this session, and it is one of my favorites in the whole archive. From your holy works, Hatonn says, a great and important man came to be healed, a general with leprosy. The prophet told him to go wash in the river seven times. And this important man was offended. It was not a grand enough cure for a man of his importance. He expected grandeur. In the end he swallowed his pride, washed in the river, and was healed.

Whenever you catch yourself gazing at a brother or a sister and feeling the distance between you, Hatonn says, whenever you feel yourself standing on some great height of intellect or knowledge or spirituality, know for certain that an opportunity for humility is coming. And when it comes, greet it with as much enthusiasm as you can muster, he says, for it is a valuable way of learning the ways of love.

That is the thread running through the whole evening. The ordinary child. The offended general. The people who seem to know less than you. All of them are doorways into the same room. We are all crawling somewhere, and none of us is above the crawl. What matters is not how fast you move, or how far, but whether you are moving at all, and whether you can love the ones moving beside you, wherever they happen to be.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Straight and Narrow
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the straight and narrow.

On the eleventh of February, in nineteen eighty-two, the evening belonged mostly to the one called Laitos, and to the doubts of new channels. One instrument after another kept wondering whether they were truly receiving, or only imagining. And Laitos answered them with something I did not expect. Do not throw your doubts away, he said. Doubt is a very important part of your seeking. Without doubt, one does not question, and to find answers, you must question not only others, but yourself.

Then came the question of the evening, carried in a letter from a brother the questioner loved. The brother had studied yogic philosophy for many years. He wanted to return to the source, which he understood to be the ninth density. His question was plain. Could he skip all the densities in between and go straight back in this lifetime?

I think of him with real affection. That burning earnestness, that desire to leap straight to the end. Laitos was kind to him and did not budge. The path of spiritual evolution, he said, must be one which is straight and narrow, and of some considerable length. It travels through many illusions and many densities, with one goal, becoming one with the Creator.

Each density, Laitos explains, gives the seeker a greater intensity of light. And when the cycle of incarnations in any density is complete, the entity is bathed in the light of the Creator until it can no longer withstand or use the increasing intensity of that light. It stops where it falls. And that is where it continues its study, in the place that matches the light it could hold.

Listen to how he puts it, because there is something so quietly devastating in it. Few upon your planet, he says, could withstand the light of the fourth density. It is a quantum leap beyond what you now experience. If any entity felt it for a single moment and could withstand it, that entity would feel indeed that it had returned to its source, and would be quite appreciative of the experience. Which is to say, the end you are rushing toward is already waiting at the end of the road you are trying to skip.

He does not scold the brother for wanting to go faster. To desire to progress as rapidly as possible is quite commendable, he says. But it is most necessary, he says, and here his voice almost smiles, to learn to walk before one runs, or flies, or soars beyond the start. Yours is a density, he says, in which the child learns to crawl. Rejoice in the opportunities that are given you.

There is a second teaching in this session, about the unblocking of energy centers, and it is worth carrying home with you. The incarnation, Laitos says, is an opportunity to accept, to forgive, to love all beings, all experiences, all events, including the self. And the way to do it in meditation is to take whatever feeling you cannot accept, and intensify it until you see its logical end. He gives the example of anger. Anger increasing to violence. Violence to pain and suffering. Pain and suffering to remorse. Remorse to a desire to make retribution. And that desire leading, at last, to a feeling of love and acceptance. Follow the feeling all the way through, and it carries you home.

What a lovely pair of teachings for one evening. Do not discard your doubts. Do not rush past your density. The path is straight and narrow and long, and every step of it is the destination, wearing a disguise.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Blossoming Light
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the blossoming light.

It is the fourteenth of February, nineteen eighty-two, and Hatonn comes with thanks on his lips and spring on his mind. He has been speaking with this group for a long time, by human reckoning, and he says he feels as much a pupil as any of them. Through them, he says, he has also learned, and has been aided in his journey. Then he turns his gaze toward the season. Spring is at hand. New growth will stretch and reach for the light, will bask in the warmth, and will fulfill its purpose.

And here is where the teaching begins, because he is not really talking about the plants. You, my friends, he says, are reaching, stretching, ever attempting to expose more and more of yourselves to the light, to the love of the Creator. In this illusion you are slowly, steadily, fulfilling your purpose, attempting to be a part of the whole. As you become more aware of the love that is within and without, as you blossom and grow, the radiance of yourself shines increasingly brighter.

I want to pause on that phrase. The radiance of yourself. Not a light you borrowed. Not a light you earned. The radiance of yourself, shining brighter simply because you are growing toward the light, the way new growth leans toward the sun without being taught.

And then he says the thing I keep coming back to. You cannot hide it, he says. It is part of you, and it is there for others to see. Whether they appreciate it or not. Whether they become like it, or seek to ignore it, or even to destroy it. The light that is you shines.

Which raises the question of what to do with such a light, and Hatonn's answer is quiet and wise. He does not ask them to preach, or to be conspicuous, or to drag anyone along into their particular way of growth. He hopes only that each, by example, may start a small spark in others. Not flash in front of people, he says. Merely allow the love and light that is you to shine, so that others may see, and deal with it as is their way.

There is a second movement to this session, and it deepens the first. Picture the Earth, Hatonn says. The creatures of it know they are part of one creation and do not question it. But your peoples, he says, have reared up and walked away from the mother, away from the felt unity of things. And yet, just as the roots of trees intertwine and touch in their search for light, so do all the creatures of your world touch each other. The air circulates among you. The chairs you sit in touch the floor. You are one, my friends, he says, and that is the fundamental function of meetings such as this.

We do not suggest, he is careful to add, that you are better than your fellow man, or wiser, or more to be. For you are your fellow man.
