But each of you has made a simple and sometimes devastating choice, which is to pursue the path of spiritual seeking. It is an adventure, and it often makes you feel immensely alone. That is why you gather. Not to become superior. To touch. As the floor and the chairs and the air touch all of you physically, so your seeking lets you feel the touch of caring, of sharing, of a kind of honor which is not the property of those who yet sleep.

And then the image he leaves them with, which I think is one of the loveliest practical teachings in the archive. Charge your batteries here, he says. Fill yourself with love and light in meditation, for there will be those who drain you out in the world. And when you go among them, know that nothing good comes from you. It comes only through you. Keep the feeling in your heart, and as you try to express love in your daily life, attempt only to be.

Attempt only to be. Blossom. Grow. Let the radiance of yourself shine, and trust it to do what shining does.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Choice Is Yours
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the choice is yours.

On the twenty-first of February, nineteen eighty-two, Hatonn spoke about compassion, and about the one thing nobody can take from you. In your illusion, he said, you are constantly faced with choices, and each one affects not only you, but also, directly or indirectly, those around you. And in this illusion, few things are simple. There is no case, he says, in which the line can be clearly drawn between the serving of others and the serving of the self.

What do you do, then, with a lifetime of such choices? You flow, he says. You act in the way that you deem most appropriate. You will find your relationships, your friendships, your family ties, weighing ever more heavily upon your decisions. And as you grow, he says, something beautiful happens. You begin to think and act first for them instead of first for you. That love and compassion extends beyond your immediate circle, reaching further and further outward, until a few begin to place all others first. But the choices are hard. Meditation, he says, can make the mind clearer, and the choices a little easier. No one but you may make your decision. The choice is always yours. No matter what acts upon you, you choose.

Then Hatonn draws a picture of two kinds of people, and it is one of the sharpest pieces of social observation in the archive. On one side, he says, there are the lonely people who do not believe they have any choice at all. First the parents instruct and must be obeyed. Then society instructs and its codes must be followed. Then a marriage, and the mate requires certain behaviors, and children come, and responsibilities pile up, until from birth to death it feels like there is no freedom, only a sometimes happy and sometimes dreary round of fitting in and doing your duty.

On the other side, he says, there are those who have listened to their inner voices and say, quite rightly, that all they need to know is already within them. Why should I accept being happy and sad and tangled up with others, they ask, when I already know all there is to know, when I already feel the light of the Creator guiding my footsteps? What need have I for further experience in the outer world?

Between these two systems of thought, Hatonn says, lies a lifetime full of choices. And he has hard words for the first group and a gentle challenge for the second. Those who believe they are not free to make choices are lazy, he says. There is no situation so limiting that you do not have full choice over your own mind, your own attitude, your own ability to radiate the love and the light of the infinite Creator. Even a prison cannot take that from you.

To those who feel they need no experience, he offers a mirror. Look back over your past, he says. Are you the same person you were? Have not your choices, one by one, added up to a transformed person, sitting in meditation in this room, on this evening, with this group of people? No matter that the universe is potentially complete within you. You must choose to know yourself, and there are so many things you cannot know without experience. In happy times and in sad, you know yourself better and better.

And then the teaching turns inward, and it becomes the most important sentence of the evening. Your first aid, he says, is to yourself, so that you may become a person capable of aiding others. And this aid is to know yourself. Not to know what others think of you. Not to know what society expects of you. Not to know what is legal. But to know what you think, what you feel, and who you are.

He does not pretend this is simple. Each entity, he says, has a light side and a dark one. To know yourself is the important thing. To know, to accept, and to love yourself, that which you consider good and that which you consider bad, is to become ready to know, to love, and to accept others. For you have a vast storehouse within you, he says, which will be of great aid as you seek the light. Meditate, that the things too deep for conscious thought may be contacted and used.

The choices are hard, and the choices are yours. That is the whole of it. Nobody can make them for you, not even the ones who love you, not even the voices from the archive. But you are never without the storehouse, and you are never without the choice.

Thank you for listening.

title: Out on a Limb
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: out on a limb.

On the twenty-fifth of February, nineteen eighty-two, in an intensive meditation session, the evening belonged to the new channels. The one called Laitos spoke first, with tenderness, about what it means to lend your voice. And then Hatonn took up the subject, answering a young instrument who was afraid his contact was polluted, afraid he was imagining it all.

Laitos begins with something I wish every creative person could hear. Each channel, he says, speaks the message in their own way, through their own vocabulary, their own background, their own store of knowledge. Each message may sound different from one channel to another, but the differences in the words are not as important as the basic meaning of the whole. One may use words others do not know, and say no more than the one whose vocabulary is small. Each is unique, he says, and each has their purpose. Do not measure yourself against another's voice.

Then Hatonn turns to the young instrument's doubt, and what he says is the heart of the whole session. The desire to be an instrument, he says, is the key ingredient in this process. But being overly concerned about your success is the most detrimental thing to your steady development. Set yourself a simple signal, he suggests, a level of the conditioning vibration, and when you feel it, simply speak, without concern for what will follow.

And then he says the sentence this episode is named for. Each time you endeavor to do this, he says, you are playing the fool, for you are out on a limb, so to speak, without assurance that the limb will hold you. Release your doubts, he says, and simply take part in the process. Speak the thoughts as you become aware of them, and you shall clear the way for the thoughts which follow. And the limb, he promises, shall indeed support you, as it has thus far.

I love that image because it is not only about channeling. Anyone who has ever tried to speak something true before they were sure it was true has stood on that limb. The teaching is not to be certain. The teaching is to speak, and let the speaking make the way.

There is a lovely exchange later in the session that I want to fold in. A sister asks, with real feeling, how many people on this planet are calling for the kind of messages this group receives. Hatonn answers with numbers that take my breath away. The Sunday meditations, with their simple message of love and the original Thought of the Creator, answer a calling expressed by roughly six hundred million entities. The deeper, intensive portions, the question and answer sessions, the seeking of wisdom and light, are called for by something approaching two hundred million. You are not alone in this, he is saying. The hunger you feel is shared by multitudes you will never meet.

And when the sister asks whether they may publish these humble messages, editing out the mechanical parts, Hatonn's answer is pure generosity. What you do with this information is completely your decision, he says. Some bathe in the moment of the message and are washed free of it. Others soak in it so it may be carried within. Others take what has become part of them and radiate it to those who never heard it firsthand. We are pleased at any choice, he says. Consent to any use you might make of these humble offerings.

Out on the limb, with the desire as your key, the signal as your reassurance, and the message free to anyone who asks. That is the whole craft of it. Speak the thoughts as you become aware of them. The limb will hold.

Thank you for listening.

title: Destroy the Pedestal
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: destroy the pedestal.

On the twenty-sixth of February, nineteen eighty-two, a Friday evening, Hatonn came with a message about the one known to you as Jesus, known to himself, Hatonn says, as Amira. And the message is not worship. It is something much more demanding than worship.

This man, Hatonn says, sought not to found a religion, a dynasty, or a kingdom on Earth, but to be of service to those who wanted to free themselves from the illusion that had begun to bind them so tightly. And then he says the sentence that quietly dismantles two thousand years of pedestal-building. It may be said, he says, that this man was no greater than any other that has walked your planet. For his accomplishment was, in simple terms, to do that which he intended upon entering your density.

And then the question, aimed gently at every listener. Was this not the same purpose for which you yourselves entered this density?

I want to stay with this a moment, because it is so easy to miss how radical it is. The accomplishment of setting yourself a task and striving toward its completion does not place you beyond the realm in which you function, Hatonn says. It more clearly defines the realm in which others may accomplish their own set tasks. And it illuminates the falsehood of accepting your supposed limitations. He once said, all of these things you shall do, and more. And Hatonn asks why we find it so convenient to ignore that statement. Because, he says, it comes uncomfortably close to reminding us of the truth of the understanding within our souls.

It is far easier, he says, to establish a towering pedestal upon which to place such leaders, such lovers, far beyond our reach and far out of our sight, so that we may not be uncomfortably reminded of our potential for attainment.

Listen to how he puts that. We do not put them on pedestals to honor them. We put them on pedestals to protect ourselves from the demand their example makes on us. The pedestal is not reverence. It is an alibi.

And so he asks for the pedestal to come down. The possibility exists at this moment, he says, for each of you to destroy the pedestal, and to realize that the accomplishments of this man and others like him are not safely out of reach, but within your grasp, within your attainment. For those individuals are yourselves, and their attainment is your own.

Then the closing charge, and it lands like a bell. The temptation exists, he says, to point at others of accomplishment and say, yes, I will be like that some day, but not yet. Be like that today, my friends. Have confidence. Have faith in yourselves. You are, as that scripture stated, yourselves sons of God, portions of the Creator. Not merely children, he says, but each a unit of light within itself.

If the Creator formed each of you as a likeness of itself, he asks, then who but yourselves are responsible for what you have created? It is a fearsome question and a liberating one, both at once. The pedestal is gone. There is nothing between you and the work except your own willingness to begin it today.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Beloved Voice
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the beloved voice.

On the twenty-eighth of February, nineteen eighty-two, Hatonn reached into one of your holy books and drew out a scene. It is called the Transfiguration. The teacher known as Jesus was seen illuminated, brightened, and those around him heard a voice that said, this is my beloved son. Listen to him.

And then Hatonn does what he always does with these stories. He turns them around until they are pointing at you. As you progress in your search, he says, you must at one point come to grips with the fact that within you lies a portion of that same consciousness which the one known as Jesus exemplified. And not only within you. Within every individual. The creation itself, he says, wood and flower, bird and bush, are sons and daughters of the Creator.

But the teaching is not only about what is true. It is about the one hard thing. Do you listen? This, Hatonn says, is the great and important part of experience. The opportunity to listen. To inwardly digest. To transfer each word and thought and vision you see into that which shows you a face, an aspect, of the one infinite Creator.

How difficult it is, he admits, to change your perceptions, for your illusion is a harsh one. It is nearly impossible to believe that the entities seated in this room are all one being. Can you not touch each other and feel the difference between you? And yet, he says, this very experience is an experience of unity. If you can hold the overview that you are speaking to yourself, that you as a portion of the creation speak only to other portions of the creation, your life will be transformed.

And then the turn inward, which is where this session becomes personal. It is easier, he says, for many of you to see the beauty and the radiance of perfection in another's being than to appreciate the perfection of your own. How many times this day, he asks, have you been dissatisfied not with others, but with yourself?

The voice said, this is my son, listen to him. Listen to yourself, my friends, Hatonn says. As well as to all the profound works of inspiration. Listen to your body. Listen to your mind. Listen to your seeking. And find the unity and the perfection at the heart of all these things. And try, he says, with such tenderness, to be pleased with the portion of creation that is yourself.

Do not cease to open yourself to the radiance that lies waiting, he says, for the one who has stopped quibbling with the self, and has instead offered the self, imperfect as it may seem, to the Creator, as a channel for love.

There is a second discourse in this session, and it is one of the starkest passages in the archive. To remain in this illusion is such a waste of your time, Hatonn says. Time is a prison. Space, a jail. All the things your society expects of you are the warden's clanking of keys as they walk past your cell. Even those who love you most expect things of you, and you expect things of them, and so you jail each other with your expectations, in small ways, every day.

You entered this relationship with the illusion for a reason, he says. To gain experience. So do not let the experience go to waste. Do not remain in prison, not in thought and not in action. Go instead into that infinite space, that infinite time, which is the kingdom. Meditate, he says, and enter it with joy, for it is a freedom you may never find within this illusion.

The beloved voice said, listen to him. The beloved voice in you is saying the same thing now. Listen.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Straying Lamb
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the straying lamb.

On the fifth of March, nineteen eighty-two, Hatonn told a story. It is a small story, and I think it may be one of the most beautiful parables in the archive. It is about a lamb.

The lamb had strayed from the flock, from its mother, from the shepherd, whose efforts to keep it safe were circumvented by the lamb's curiosity. The lamb had realized that among the flock it was simply retracing the steps already covered by those around it, and it chose to wander further and further toward the edge of the flock, seeking experience beyond what could be narrated by its elders.

As it moved toward the edge, Hatonn says, the lamb noticed that the sheep out there were different. Still sheep, but of a more unencumbered nature. Less interested in the close, shoulder to shoulder life of the center. Often one would stop, snatch a bite, look about, and have to gallop to regain the safety of the flock. Those at the perimeter were a different breed of sheep.

But the lamb was not satisfied with a change of scenery. Upon reaching the edge of the flock, it continued beyond the flock, beyond the shepherd, beyond all that was known and familiar. Gradually the sound of the flock diminished. And the lamb was alone, having abandoned its past.

Perhaps at this point, Hatonn says, one would assume the lamb should be afraid. It is well known that the world contains those which prey upon the innocent, upon those who extend themselves beyond the edge of the flock. Yet the lamb, possessing the wise naiveté of the fool, was not troubled. For the lamb simply sought to know.

I love that phrase. The wise naiveté of the fool. It holds the whole teaching. The fool is not wise because he knows the dangers. He is wise because his desire to know is stronger than his fear of them.

Hatonn leaves the story there, deliberately. The lamb, he says, is still wandering, further and further from the crowded security it left behind, where the decisions are made by caretakers. And then he turns to his listeners. The lambs within your souls seek only to learn, he says, and it is that craving for knowledge, for new experience with which to grow, that has brought you here this night.

There is a meekness in knowledge, he says, for an early and constant lesson upon that path is the awareness that one's knowledge is sorely lacking. The path extends ever onward, to that knowledge which is without end.

And then he answers the question he knows is forming in every mind. To what purpose do we wander, if there is no reward at the end, no pot of gold at the terminus of the rainbow? Why leave the flock? Is it not safer within the confinement of the crowd? My friends, he says, you are wanderers of the path, and to do other than that would betray your real nature. Accept this in yourselves, and be not afraid. For though the predators exist, so also does that force within your world that knows of each bird in flight, of each tree desiring to bloom, of each flower striving through the soil toward the sun.

Follow your path consciously and joyfully, he says. And if you find other lambs upon your path, be grateful for the God that walks beside you. For each of you is of the Creator, a facet, a particle of that which you call God, and each of you follows the path that guides you back to your Creator self.

The lamb is still wandering. So are you. That is not a failure of the story. That is the story.

Thank you for listening.

title: Out of Your Own Way
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: out of your own way.

On the seventh of March, nineteen eighty-two, a Sunday evening, Hatonn spoke about purity. And the first thing you should know is that he does not mean what your peoples usually mean by it. Purity, he says, is the non-resistance to the outward shining of light from the individual.

Every molecule, every atom, every portion of substance in your universe, being a facet of the Creator, is imbued with the light of the Creator, and is capable of projecting that light in all directions. But your individualized consciousness exerts a controlling influence over how much light your vehicle emits. Which is to say, you have the ability to restrict the light you give back. And when you do, Hatonn says, you do not only dim yourself. Taken across your whole race, this restriction lowers the vibratory level of your planet, and that is the root of the physical and emotional traumas your peoples continually experience.

He reaches for your holy texts. The saying about hiding one's light beneath a basket refers to exactly this choice. It is within your power to restrict the light you return to the Creator, and to restrict the growth of your brothers and sisters along with it. There is pressure all around you to conform, to avoid standing out. But he asks you to consider whether a greater service might be performed by being brave enough to let your light shine forth fully. There is no being in existence, he says, who can resist the beneficial effects of that.

Then Latwii takes up the theme, and his sermon on purity is one of the most charming passages in the archive. Purity, he says, is as simple as light. Look out your window in the early morning, he says. The tiny crocuses moving upward toward the still cool spring sun. They are pure. The squirrels chasing the birds from the seed you put out, bright eyes darting, tails moving cleverly as they keep their balance. The song of the birds. All pure, he says. They are pure because they are not conscious of themselves. They are what they are, without question.

But you, he says, with such warmth, have been given a complicated task. To find again that beingness, that feeling of being part of the creation with no effort, while you are conscious of yourself. And then the sentence this episode is named for. Your greatest task, my friends, he says, is to stay out of your own way. For that which you are will shine, and all that might obstruct it is that which you might do.

I want to read that again slowly, because it undoes so much striving. You are already a being of perfect love and light, he says. To stay out of your way is a tremendous service to yourself and to others. All the intelligence and analysis you can produce through your whole incarnation cannot yield one more iota of light than the totality of your being to begin with.

So go within, he says, and trust that what you are to be or do is least of all a function of the mind that analyzes, and far more truly a function of your ability to feel comfortable being one who is loved totally by the Creator. If you are loved, you can then love, no matter what other function you may have in this illusion. Love, my friends, he says, is the heart of your gift to those about you, and to yourself.

One more thread from this long evening, because it belongs with the theme. A sister asks about the beings called angels, the guardians who watch over each entity. Latwii answers that each of you does call for assistance, whether consciously or not, and each calling is answered. Many answers come in sleep and dreams. Many come as hunches that seem to arrive out of the blue. Many come as coincidences, as the right person appearing with the right piece of your solution at the right moment. At all times, he adds, each entity is in harmony with the Creator. The only thing that changes is your conscious awareness of it.

Stay out of your own way. Let the light that is already yours do what light does. And when help comes, in whatever quiet form, let yourself receive it.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Tools of Emotion
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the tools of emotion.

On the twelfth of March, nineteen eighty-two, Hatonn spoke briefly, and his message was about the one thing we are all carrying and none of us quite knows how to hold. Our emotions.

It is difficult at times, he begins, to share with one another our feelings of confusion or sorrow, for these emotions come from an awareness that we cannot balance our perceptions of the universe we live in. And because they are based on confusion, they are understandably hard to describe. He sympathizes, he says, with how dismaying the illusion can be. But then he draws the line that gives this session its spine. The responsibility for clarifying this confusion, he says, resides with the individual. If it is your desire to perceive your illusion clearly, then it is your responsibility to see that your perceptions come from reality, and not from the illusion.

Your perceptions of your reality, he continues, substantially affect how you relate to your other selves, and therefore the results of all your efforts toward service. It is essential, he says, to develop the ability to control your emotional reflexes. And then the image. The emotions you experience are tools, he says, which may aid or retard your development, depending on your willingness and skill in learning to use them.

Listen to how he puts it, because it is so vivid. As you become more adept, you will realize that in your recent past you were in the position of the malleable iron, being hammered into a convoluted shape by the tools of emotion, instead of being able to use those same tools for the development of your service orientation.

The iron and the tools are the same. Only the hands change. Hatonn urges you to be conscious of your use of these tools, for like so many things your peoples manipulate, they may cause harm as well as good in the hands of the unskilled.

Latwii's portion of the evening picks up the same thread from the other end, in a question about tolerance. How do you bear it, a sister asks, when someone does the opposite of what you wish they would do? And Latwii answers with a question of his own. Examine the wish first, he says. The desire to manipulate another into the behavior you prefer may be attractive, but it does not serve your growth, whether you do the manipulating yourself or merely wish some catalyst would do it for you.

The better route, he says, is to look at the behavior that irritates you and try to understand why it stirs an unpleasing emotion in you. Look within your own soul for the origin of these negative feelings, he says, and try to extend forgiveness to the one whose actions you took as a wrong. It is difficult, he admits, to get emotional and spiritual distance from the lessons you attract, for they will pursue you across the face of the Earth until you are willing to accept the catalyst you requested. The irritant is not the problem. The irritant is the teacher.

And one more teaching from this evening, for those who are afraid in meditation. A sister describes becoming frightened when she sits alone, and Latwii tells her plainly that there are entities who disrupt the efforts of those polarizing toward the positive, projecting fear and disruptive thoughts. His remedy is the remedy that runs through the whole archive. Direct love and light toward whoever is sending the disruption, he says. After a short time you will find the disruptions reduce in frequency and intensity, for your return gift is quite uncomfortable for its recipients.

Tools, all of them. The emotions in your own chest. The irritation another person stirs in you. The fear that visits your meditation. None of them are masters. They are instruments, waiting for a hand that knows what it is doing. The work is to become that hand.

Thank you for listening.

title: The New Lights
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the new lights.

On the fourteenth of March, nineteen eighty-two, Hatonn spoke about children. Not as projects, not as blank slates, but as lights. New lights, he calls them, arriving on the planet at the most consequential moment of its history.

The season has changed, he begins. New life will soon begin, each entity seeking the light, each wishing its own place in the whole of creation. And each of these new entities now incarnating, he says, has an excellent chance of reaching what he calls the harvest. They will have an impact on your planet, and they will demand a great deal from those around them. They will teach, he says, as well as be taught.

Cherish the new life, he says. For each life is a beginning, and a means for all to see.

Then he turns to the parents, and what he says will undo a great deal of what your society taught you about raising children. It is thought, he says, that the parent writes upon a blank slate, constructing the mind and behavior of the offspring. But these new lights, he says, are in many ways old lights. They have been among you since time in your dimension began. Those entering now are very likely entities of great experience and learning. Be aware, he says, that those whom you would teach may have come to assist you in learning, to aid you in achieving the level of service you need.

It is said on your planet, he reminds them, that the child is the father to the man. There are many depths of meaning in that statement, he says, and he encourages everyone present to meditate upon it.

And then, with disarming humor, he punctures the whole solemn business of parenthood. Each of you remembers, he says, being a small and defenseless being under the protection of those seemingly godlike entities called grownups, and more especially parents. And then time passes, and you discover that you have become those very large beings whose iron rule was once totally accepted, and you find, my friends, that you are only large. You have not become omniscient, or impervious, or full of wisdom.

He laughs with them about it, and then gives them the one thing that matters. None, small or large, is infallible, he says. But there is one thing that can be done, and he speaks not only to parents but to all. Always seek the original Thought of the one infinite Creator. In seeking this heart within yourself and within the creation, you bring sunshine into a life that might otherwise seem random and uninteresting.

He gives them two images to carry home, and both are worth keeping. The first is weaving. You may look at your being as that which is woven, he says. Most people go to the market and buy what is offered, cheaply or for style. But few plan the design of their weaving and then go select the yarns. If you weave your inner life slowly and thoughtfully, he says, the pattern that emerges will speak far more loudly to child, to friend, or to stranger than any momentary behavior.

The second is the piano. Think of a lifetime as something played on the piano, he says. You can sit on the keys and make a jangle. You can play the same little tune over and over until you are the last one tired of it. You can learn to entertain. Or you can acquaint yourself with the literature of the instrument, gain the technique, and then select the tune which carries your life in its breath.

These children being born now, he says, are old souls, and dealing with them is not always child's play. They have chosen their parents, and you have chosen them, for very specific reasons. To comfort each other. To teach each other. And above all, my friends, to love each other.

And for those who are not parents, he leaves this. All who live at this time can be parents in the metaphysical sense, nurturing those whom you meet, comforting, accepting, loving. Do not be displeased with yourself over momentary lapses. The great gift you give, he says, is always yourself. Your carefully woven tapestry of being. The lovely lilting melody you have chosen to play with your life.

Soft and gentle as raindrops, he says, is the love that surrounds you.

Thank you for listening.

title: Your Own Song
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: your own song.

On the twenty-first of March, nineteen eighty-two, Hatonn opened with something tender. He said he was happy to hear their voices seeking to harmonize with one another, to bring forth song. And then he gave them the teaching that the image was carrying. Each sings the same words, he said, yet each feels and expresses those same words in sometimes subtle and at other times very distinct ways. From the one source came many variations.

Each of you is here to become aware, he says, but what each needs is not the same. Each treads their own path, though you be one in spirit. So do not feel lacking, he says, and do not doubt your growth, if you are not doing as you see your brothers or sisters doing. Your path is your own. Follow it as it may lead. Keep your eyes forward and go as the light leads.

Your path will cross the paths of many others, he says, and at times they may be shared, and these times are always joyous, for they show you that you are not alone. There are others who will help, whom you may help. But worry not if the paths diverge. Walk on. Share when you may. Give what you can. Be not proud, and deny not what others wish to share.

And then the sentence this episode is named for. If the need be felt, he says, raise your voice in chorus with others. But be not afraid to stand alone and sing.

I love that he does not resolve the tension. The chorus and the solitary voice are both holy. The group is real, and the path is your own, and you will need both, and neither one will excuse you from the other.

The second movement of his discourse is about the gifts we bring to these gatherings, and it is built around a story your peoples know well. Many gathered around the teacher known as Jesus, Hatonn says, and his disciples were uneasy, for they wished to feed the thousands and had little food and less money. The one known as Jesus broke and scattered what seemed to be not enough, and it was more than enough.

You, my friends, are also filled with this bread, Hatonn says. It has been called the bread of heaven. It may seem to you that it is not enough. But oh, my friends, what an infinity of bounty you possess. This gathering, he tells them, exists for one purpose. To send you forth alone into a world sorely in need of the wholeness and purity of the love of the infinite Creator.

You may feel that the love you felt here belongs to the group, that you cannot carry it out alone. But you are only resonating together with one common vibration, he says, the great original vibration of light. And this you can take with you. As you follow your path in the light, in service, remembering the Creator, you become yourself an offering to the world, a manifestation of this enormous creative love, without saying any word or making any gesture.

You cannot do this yourself, he admits, for you are as you are in this illusion. But there is that within you which is more yourself than the self you now know. And that deeper self can love. It can show patience and understanding. And, my friends, it can sing alone in the darkness, and offer to those who grope for love the beacon that may guide them to their own paths, toward light.

Go from this place, then, he says, and trust in the plenty and the bounty of love. Find it in meditation again and again, that you may do the things you wish to do in wholeness, in purity, in love. That you may sing your song with a glad and cheerful heart.

The chorus is beautiful. But the song is yours. Do not be afraid to sing it alone.

Thank you for listening.

title: The First Baby Steps
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the first baby steps.

On the twenty-second of March, nineteen eighty-two, Hatonn came to an intensive meditation with practical help for a struggling instrument. The one known as C had become so sensitive to the contact that he could no longer recognize it, and Hatonn, with great patience, proposed a simple signal. A small opening of the mouth, he said, somewhat as a yawn would feel, though without the deep breathing. A gentle mechanical movement, to tell the instrument that contact had been made, and that it was safe to speak.

What moves me about this is the care in it. Hatonn does not demand confidence the instrument does not have. He builds a bridge the instrument can actually cross. And then he gives the principle behind the bridge. It is very meritorious, he says, that the instrument not speak if there is doubt as to the origin of the contact. It is far better to remain tuned and silent than to accept a possible detuning by channeling an entity of whose identity you are not sure.

Then the discourse widens, and it becomes a message for every seeker, not only the channels. To speak to you for what to you has been a long time, Hatonn says, has been a great source of joy and of learning for us. The message we have, he says, is always the same. But always a new facet is shown, that you may take each one and meditate upon it, and add it to the others, and become aware that by summation of the parts you may see that the whole is greater than the sum of the parts can ever be.

The love and the light of the infinite Creator, he says, is beyond anything your language can give, beyond what we or you now see. You become aware in your vision of only a small part of that light and love. But as with all things in your illusion, the first step needs to be taken. The choice must begin to be made. The path chosen.

Now take what may be said to be your first baby steps, he says, the first few steps along the long but joyous path back to the One. Remember always that there is ever so much more to learn than you can see in your illusion. Your perception is limited by your physical vehicle, and by how much of your mind has been awakened. But you shall know. You shall learn. You shall be aware.

Take your steps carefully, he says. And if you stumble and fall, be not proud and refuse the help of others. If help is needed, allow them to help you stand once again, that you may continue to take the small but important steps.

You are not alone, he says, as we are not alone. There are countless kindred souls who reach out, who wish to help, who wish to give. They are not too proud to receive. They are with you, brothers and sisters.

The signal. The silence when in doubt. The baby steps. The hand offered when you fall. The whole spiritual path, in one short evening, made small enough to begin tonight.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Constant Giving
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the constant giving.

On the twenty-sixth of March, nineteen eighty-two, Hatonn spoke about giving. And the first thing he wants you to unlearn is the shape you think giving has. Too often, he says, giving is regarded as a finite act, a sort of stopgap effort. He gives the image of a gear on a watch that at regular intervals detains a rotating wheel, preventing a surge of energy from bursting out of control. Many on your planet, he says, regard giving as a way of temporarily preventing their lives from spinning uselessly out of control, by the periodic application of spiritual brakes.

Giving, he says, extends much further than that. There is a point at which the act of giving can be regarded as finite, thus limiting its effect. And there is a point at which the same act may produce an infinite amount of effects, all oriented toward the service of your brothers and sisters. It is said on your planet that it is better to give than to receive, he says, because receiving is a simple service to another, while giving can and should be a constant and daily process, woven through everything you do to take part in your illusion.

He gives them an example they can see every day. Many present, he says, serve as assistants for the physical, emotional, and educational maturation of recently arrived members of your race. A mother, for example, may spend an entire day engrossed in giving to her young, whose requirements for attention are quite stringent. And the pattern of her giving is not a jerky stopgap punctuating her day. It flows continuously, from early morning until late night, and as we have noticed, he adds with gentle humor, regrettably late into the night and early into the morning as well.

It is one of the lessons of your experience, he says, that this continuous flow of giving may be extended beyond the obvious needs of the young child, to the more subtle needs of the individuals you meet through your waking hours, often strangers. It is possible, he says, to spend an entire day performing a myriad of services for literally hundreds of individuals, thus reinforcing the ties that will eventually link each of you to your fellow members of the developing social memory complex.

Wishing good morning to a stranger. Holding a door open. Picking up an object another has dropped. These may all be combined, he says, into a major accomplishment. And what unifies these seemingly insignificant events into a continuous flow of giving is the conscious, though generally unspoken, expression of love for those you encounter, combined with the loving acceptance of those same individuals.

Then he takes up the saying your peoples know as judge not, lest you be judged, and gives it a reading I had never considered. The act of judgment, he says, is the act of separating yourself and the other from the developing complex. You place yourself in the role of judge, and the other in the role of the one found insufficient. You step out of the family to point at the family. So he urges them to abandon the seat of judgment, and take instead the position of a loving member of the family, the unified group struggling to attain the unification of intention, wisdom, and compassion.

There is a lovely companion teaching in the question and answer portion of this evening. A brother asks about the rituals of the ancients, the ceremonies and the substances used to contact the divine. Latwii answers that the purpose of any ritual is simply to function as a tool, and the tool is designed and selected by its owner to fulfill a specific need. If you wish to communicate with the Creator, he says, simply address yourself, your brother or sister, or any object within reach. For all are a part of the Creator.

And when the same brother keeps looking backward, asking about a sighting from his childhood some twenty years past, Latwii gives him counsel worth keeping. The signposts are not the road, he says. Many events in life are like signposts assisting you along a predetermined route. But the experiences of most individuals are to travel in small circles, not realizing the signposts exist. Perceive the signposts as just that, he says, and concentrate on the road ahead instead.

Give continuously. Judge rarely. And keep your eyes on the road, not on the signposts behind you.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Tree Gives Shade
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the tree gives shade.

On the twenty-eighth of March, nineteen eighty-two, Hatonn spoke about compassion, a term, he said, not fully understood by your peoples, and difficult to express in words. And then, to express it, he told a story.

The hero of the story is a man bent upon learning the meaning of compassion. He seeks first a very famous and successful spiritual guide. This famous man greets him in a palatial home, his manner most civilized, his whole being radiating the confidence of wealth. And the rich man explains his philosophy. All these things I own are necessary, he says, that I may offer my services to those who in turn have the power to help so many others. True compassion, he says, is knowing where to put your energies. I have offered my aid to those who will be able, in turn, to be of the greatest help to the greatest number.

The hero leaves unsatisfied and walks into the meaner part of the city, past warehouses and bolted windows, to a dirty falling-down storefront marked mission. Inside, a gaunt woman is ladling soup for those who have no money. He asks her, with hope in his voice, can you tell me what compassion is? Certainly, she says, lifting her tired eyes from the kettle. Compassion is a plate of soup for a hungry man. Compassion is seeing beauty and perfection in those things which are apparently not lovely. In seeing love in that which is not loved.

How many do you serve, he asks. I do not know, she says. As many as I can supply with soup. Not many, I suppose. But it is all that I can do.

The seeker is confused. The two faces of compassion both seem compelling. One is logical. One moves the heart. Wandering in the afternoon sun, he comes to a tree in a small park, and sits on the circular seat beneath it to think. On one side of him sits a wealthy man, busy with his work. On the other side rests one of the men from the soup kitchen, unable to function within a society based on money. The seeker looks up at the tree, Hatonn says, and suddenly knows what compassion is. For the tree is shading all three of them from the harshness of the afternoon sun.

My friends, Hatonn says, in compassion there is no judgment. The actions you take because of your compassion may be many and various. But the love within you, if you wish to be compassionate, shall shine as gently as sunlight filtered through the living green of the shading leaves of a great tree.

Before the story, Hatonn had laid the groundwork, and I want to give it to you plainly. Do not treat yourself harshly, he said, when you fall short of your expectations of how you should help others, or when others fail to respond as you hoped. The attempt is often worth more when it is tried without the expected results, for then you can reflect, and learn to deal with yourself softly. As you do this, you are better able to touch another softly. The softness, the touch, the warmth conveyed, tends to be a more direct linking than grabbing or pulling or pushing. One need only be open, flowing, to be in touch with another, and to see more clearly from the perspective of the other.

So often, he says, the urge to take charge of a situation creates more blockages than existed before it. As you learn to be soft, the walls become less high, and open slowly, and allow the touching and the exchange. The softness is something you must learn to develop, though it has always been within you.

And after the story, the practice. It is not to be expected, he says, that you can hold such compassion without aid. And the aid he suggests, as always, is meditation. For these things are your birthright, locked within you as treasure within a chest, and meditation is the key. If you wish to radiate to others, he says, you must first allow the radiance within you to come forth. And if you block it with disappointment in yourself, then stop, and return to meditation, until you can see that in the view of love it matters not what mistakes or conditions or experiences you have had. It matters only that you are a portion of the infinite Creator. This is your reality. The remainder is illusion.

Be gentle with yourselves, he asks, as well as with others. And let your love touch each entity about you the way the tree touches all three men beneath it. Without choosing. Without judging. Simply shading.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Wild Flower
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the wild flower.

On the second of April, nineteen eighty-two, Hatonn came to a Friday evening circle with a message about love. Not the love songs sing about. Something older and less graspable than that.

It is the blessings of the Creator, he begins, that draw you to seek one another's companionship, to share the light that joins you, that makes a oneness of your individual alonenesses. It is the sharing of the Creator's love, although greatly misunderstood, that is perhaps the primary driving force of all striving, both spiritual and physical, upon your plane.

But here is the trouble, and he names it plainly. That desire for the light of the Creator becomes transmuted, in many, into a lesser form. Just as an alchemist might inadvertently transmute gold back into lead, he says. Those who experience this find themselves seeking the light of the Creator, yet perceiving that light as the love given by, or drawn from, another individual of your species. They mistake the vessel for the source.

Realize and be aware of the source of the love which can permeate your lives, he says. Understand that in loving another, you love yourself. And then he asks the questions that cut through every anxious negotiation of the heart. Is it your desire to imprison love within bonds of promises about the future, made with no awareness of what the future holds? Is it your desire to fashion a permanence of an emotion by establishing a rigid outer form, a structure for that emotion, like words carved into stone that persist long after what they represent has passed?

Give and accept love, he says, with the awareness that it is a precious gift which may be neither owned nor held, but simply experienced. And be grateful for this experience, he says, as one encountering a wild flower growing freely and beautifully in one of your forests. Seek not to define it, but rather appreciate the beauty that exists.

I keep returning to that wild flower. You do not pick it to prove it is yours. You do not build a fence around it to keep it safe. You kneel beside it for a moment, and then you walk on, and the flower goes on being what it is, whether you are watching or not. That is how Hatonn asks you to hold love. Freely given. Freely received. Never owned.

He turns then to the customs of your race, the bonds and institutions meant to give love permanence. The custom itself does no harm, he says. It is a tool, and like any tool, it can serve or hinder its master. The teaching is simple and easy to forget. The tool is meant to serve, he says, and not to command. The role established by the tool is but a fleeting image, form without substance, if it does not serve its purpose, which is to be a conduit through which love may flow freely in all directions.

We urge you, he says, to give freely of your love to all who would receive it. Be generous, my friends, with yourselves. For indeed, these brothers and sisters are but yourselves.

The second movement of the evening widens the lens. Your illusion often appears to you as an entrapment, he says, an endless complexity in which you have somehow ensnared yourselves. But those difficulties, those challenges, are also reflections of love. They exist in part because of conditions you established yourselves, before this incarnation, that you might learn to choose to be of service to one another, and in so doing attempt the reunification of your race into a single consciousness of love.

Some despair of this, he says, and flee to desolate places to love in a more suitable manner. Others immerse themselves in the greatest densities of population, striving to love where love is sorely lacking. Both can be paths of service, he says. Your own path will be that portion of the spectrum within which you are best able to serve. So do not concern yourselves with comparisons between your service and another's. Find your path, he says, and strive confidently to follow it.

Like the wild flower, your love was never meant to be owned, fenced, or carved in stone. It was meant to be encountered, gratefully, in passing, and given away just as freely.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Cave Within
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the cave within.

On the fourth of April, nineteen eighty-two, Hatonn took his listeners somewhere most of them did not want to go. Into a cave.

There is a cave, he says, that is a subterranean maze, full of darkness and half-darkness, and into this cave your mind so often travels. So many among your peoples fear these travels, he says, that they form an enormous majority. Their fear of these deep and secret places of their minds is such that they would do anything to avoid them. To not think. To not search. To not be awake. And so you see around you many whose intellects you know to be above adequate, working quite hard to distract themselves from that great cavern of being which lies below the surface of the comfortable, everyday illusion.

He does not pretend the journey is safe. We share with you the perception, he says, that this search through the mind for truth is risky. One does not stumble upon love and illumination and blinding joy within ten days of saying, I shall seek the truth. There is never a time, no matter how many dark places you have entered and come through safely, when you are not potentially at the entrance to another blind alley, another difficult station, another point in your growth when it will seem to you that all has come to zero, and there is no more use in seeking, and no more hope for love and laughter and easiness of heart.

But those who seek, he says, shall indeed be given what they seek. And the truth of your being is a truth of unity. Not apparent unity. Not conditional unity. But unity with the dark and with the light, with the shadow and with the angel. One love created all. One love creates you. One great Thought is you, and all else in the creation.

Do you wish to know yourself? You have many choices to make, he says, for again and again it will be easier to decide to know nothing more than to affirm your desire to know. And each affirmation will bring with it a resolution, a lightening, and often that sudden burst of joy.

He offers only the comfort you could offer a child, he says, for you are as children. As you grow there are not only scrapes and bruises but very real dangers, most of which work out quite well. See yourself in your inner journey as a child. Know yourself as naive, unsophisticated. Yet know that you are not alone, for there is always guidance, and this guidance is with you constantly.

Seek the times of quiet, he says. For all truly shall be well. Even in a night when there are no candles, the dawn comes.

That line deserves to be held for a moment. Even in a night when there are no candles, the dawn comes. It does not come because you earned it, or because you finally understood the cave. It comes because that is what dawn does.

He gives them the image of the roots. In your conversation you spoke of the planting of flowers, he says. The bloom comes and goes. Your transitory experiences bloom and fade ever so quickly, and whether the blooming is effortless or labored, it passes, and your true essence goes down again into the roots, to be nurtured, to be affirmed, and to be fed by your desire, by your faithfulness to the will to seek the love of the Creator.

The second discourse of the evening is about discouragement, and it is some of the most practical counsel in the archive. Discouragement, anticipation, joy, depression, Hatonn says, are all emotions. They are but tools that you may call upon in your quest for growth. When you sense discouragement, perceive these emotions for what they are, instruments for evaluating your progression, for adjusting what retards you, for discerning where your perception must change.

And then the practice, which I think is worth memorizing. Do not take the identity of the tool upon yourself, he says. Do not say, I am discouraged. Say instead, I sense discouragement within myself. Experience the sensation with awareness, and make use of this powerful tool to further your striving. Just as you would not look at a stalled car and say, I am a dead car.

There is no failure, he tells them. Those who set foot on the path do so by choice, the choice to seek the light. It is a choice not made lightly, and once made, cannot be abandoned. For how may a child decide at one moment never again to grow, never more to learn?

Believe in yourselves, he says. Love yourselves. And continue confidently in your efforts. The cave is dark, but it is yours, and the dawn is already on its way.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Still Quiet Voice
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the still quiet voice.

The ninth of April, nineteen eighty-two, was the day your peoples call Good Friday, the remembrance of the one known to you as Jesus, or Joshua, known to Hatonn as Amira. And Hatonn came that evening to speak about him, and about what his life actually means for yours.

The mission and accomplishments of this entity, Hatonn says, have been greatly misunderstood. An effort was made by many to interpret his words within the framework of what was earlier understood, and yet was so sorely lacking as to require his sojourn upon your planet at all. Some misunderstood him. Others made a conscious effort to misrepresent his words, to create confusion, and to swell the numbers of those who would fail to polarize at all.

But then the sentence that steadies the whole session. It is never possible, Hatonn says, for confusion to overwhelm knowledge. Just as darkness, being but the absence of light, is unable to overwhelm light.

I want to stay with that image a moment. Darkness is not a substance. It is not a force that can defeat light in battle. It is simply what is there when light has not yet arrived. All the confusion in the world, Hatonn is saying, has exactly that much power, and no more.

There is always one source of information you may draw upon, he says. And that is the still, quiet voice that speaks to you from the depths of your soul when you bring it a heartfelt question. It is often difficult to perceive that voice behind the clamorings of the mind. And for this reason, among others, he strongly encourages the frequent use of the tool you call meditation. For it is only through skill with this tool, he says, that the voice may be perceived, and thereafter recognized.

The attainments of Amira are worthy of your attention and emulation, he says. But it is important that you realize his accomplishments are not unattainable to yourselves. If anything, they are more attainable as a result of his efforts. Seek, my friends, and you shall find. Knock, and it shall be opened to you. And if you but ask, that for which you ask, you shall receive. For such is the way of the universe.

These are not, he insists, merely grand statements from a man thought to be two thousand years dead. They are statements of fact, simple laws that guide the functioning and development of your universe. If it is your will to attain the growth he achieved, if you would have his knowledge, if you would share his wisdom, then these goals are within your grasp. If your knock at the door of knowledge is ceaseless, he says, if you maintain your hunger, refusing to be satisfied with what you are aware of, and continue to strive toward what is still unknown, then your quest will be fulfilled, just as his was.

You may recall, he says, the final statement attributed to him on the day you are recalling. It is consummated. Give yourselves to your striving, Hatonn says. Do not yield to distraction, to boredom, or to the influences of those who do not understand your seeking. Maintain your efforts, and do not be satisfied until you have reached the point where you may confidently acknowledge that your task of learning on this plane is complete.

He closes with an image I did not expect and will not forget. He asks them to be aware that his own words are sometimes ponderous and unyielding, and his intention is only to serve. Just as, he says, the one who fiercely, and seemingly without compassion, braided himself a whip and drove the money changers from the place of worship. The eyes can't see it, he says, but the heart can recognize the love within the action.

Sometimes love looks like stillness. Sometimes it looks like a whip. The work is to listen past the eyes, to the still, quiet voice underneath, and to keep knocking until the door opens.

Thank you for listening.

title: He Is Not Here
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: he is not here.

On the eleventh of April, nineteen eighty-two, Easter Sunday, the circle gathered with the resurrection on their minds, and Latwii took the story in his hands and turned it toward the living.

Consider it, he says. One to whom you were deeply devoted has been killed in a most barbarous manner, and his body placed in a cave behind a great rock. It is daybreak, and you go to tend the dead. You are mourning, yet you know death, for it comes to all. But there is no corpse. And a being whiter than any normal being, and more full of light, says to you, he is not here. He is alive.

The women were afraid, Latwii says, and most troubled in mind, because the possibility of life had suddenly been presented to them. And then he asks the question that makes this session unforgettable. My friends, he says, why are you afraid of dying, and take your living for granted? Would it not be more helpful to you to have a fear and awe and wonder at the living that you are somehow miraculously doing?

So many of your peoples, he says, pass through this life in a dream, scarcely waking until they die. Let your life become less familiar to you, he says. Try to see how totally amazing it is. Find that which has been called in your holy works life more abundant. Because there is so much to do, to see, to feel. There is so much joy in the universe. Why waste a day, a moment, upon indifference?

You are all alive, he says, and you shall be, now and forever. Stand in awe of the great consciousness of the Creator, and try not to slip too quickly into indifference.

Hatonn had opened the evening with the same season in his own voice. What you celebrate at this time of year, he said, is a rebirth, a reemergence of life upon your planet and within your souls. It is fitting that the death of the one you call Jesus coincides with this time, for just as the old form that seems withered and dead is suddenly abandoned in spring, and a new life leaps forth that was unseen and inconceivable before, so it is with you. Accept, recognize, and celebrate your spring, he says. Let your hearts climb ever higher, striving to obtain the light, to take it in, to make it ever a part of you.

And just as the light is passed through the food chain on the physical realm, from plant to animal, from brother to brother, he says, so it is in the spiritual realm. Be aware of your need to share your light, and of your brother's need to partake of your light, that you may both be sustained.

Later in the evening, a sister told Latwii about an overwhelming spiritual experience she had suffered in her thirties, a presence that filled a room and left a pain in her heart for years, a pain she tried for a long time to forget. And Latwii answered her with one of the most beautiful images in the archive. The pain, he said, acts like the grain of sand within the oyster. It motivates you to ask the reasons for the occurrence, to seek its meaning, and as you seek, you produce within your being that which the grain of sand produces in the oyster. The pearl of great price.

It is often the case, he told her gently, that an experience too overwhelming to be considered at once must be spread out over a lifetime for its meaning to be fully revealed. The forgetting was not a failure. It was the slow work of the oyster.

He is not here. He is alive. And so, Latwii insists, are you, more alive than you have yet dared to notice. Let the day become unfamiliar again. Let the pain become a pearl. Do not waste a moment upon indifference.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Fragile Chain
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the fragile chain.

On the fifteenth of April, nineteen eighty-two, Hatonn came to an intensive meditation with a short message about fragility. The transcript is brief, but the teaching is whole.

Observe, he says, the seeming delicacy of all that surrounds you. The extreme delicacy of the parameters which guard the ability of your physical vehicles to dwell in safety upon this sphere in space. The fragile chain of life which the creation has provided for all creatures, from the smallest to the greatest.

And yet, he says, this seeming fragility houses an imponderably huge and immense role of an evolution which goes so far beyond the evolution of the physical form that there are no words to describe this everlasting evolution. It may seem at times that each of you is a fragile and easily wounded and torn entity. Yet there is no possibility of true harm, he says, for there is no ending to consciousness. Physical death cannot touch it. And any experience can only aid it.

I want to hold that sentence still for a moment. There is no ending to consciousness. Everything fragile about you is the costume. Everything you are is the part that cannot be torn.

It may seem, he continues, that the third-density experience carries a great loneliness, a great separation of being from being, brother from brother. We have often said that this can be gone beyond in the depths of meditation, that the roots of being and of consciousness can be seen to be one. But even in your everyday existence, he says, even in the greatest illusion possible, you may see signs of the oneness of all things.

How many times, he asks, just when you thought this illusion held no ideals, have you heard of some entity who acted in such a way that the light of the one infinite Creator radiates to the world? You will see stories upon stories of the difficulties and travails of your planet, and travails there will be, for this is the proper time for such to occur. Yet in the midst of these, you will see again and again the story of one just such as yourself, who has turned from being the sheep and has awakened into the shepherd, and tends the flock.

What might this flock be, he asks. It might be a person defending the beauty of an ideal against those who would misuse it for money or for power. It might be a person who has given much to aid a group or a cause at great personal sacrifice. Or it might be one person who serves one other person with such selflessness that all who see it may marvel. This, he says, is the creation. The illusion can be pierced.

And then the closing counsel, which belongs to anyone who has ever failed at anything. You have within you the ideals that are your birthright, he says, and you also have what the world calls travails. Accept them in yourself and in the world, these seeming imperfections. And no matter how great the error, attempt to see yourself in each circumstance that comes before your vision. Imagine yourself in the place of one who has greatly erred, and then forgive yourself. For although you have been wrong, yet you are still the child of an infinite Creator, and there is time enough, and more, to mend any error.

The chain is fragile. What it carries is not. Tend your flock, forgive your errors, and remember that nothing you truly are can ever be broken.

Thank you for listening.

title: Prepare for Joy
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: prepare for joy.

It is springtime, and Hatonn begins by listening. Not to the group, but to the birds outside the room. The singing of the birds has begun again, he says. The cycle has turned, and new life begins. If you would sit quietly and listen, the world around you would speak of many things, and you might become aware of the simple and profound lessons it offers.

This evening his subject is the future. Not prophecy, exactly, but the way the future can be spoken of at all. He wants to explain, he says, the difficulty of sending specific information through a free-will contact. What the instrument receives is not words but concepts, crystalline impressions, which the instrument then clothes in whatever vocabulary it has. A little of the instrument always enters the message, and Hatonn says they welcome that. Their simple message becomes more varied, more inspiring, for passing through a human mind.

This is why they will not give dates and places. The future, for them, is not a fixed thing to be read. It is a field of probabilities, shaped moment by moment by the free will of the people. And when a group keeps demanding specifics, other voices step in, voices quite willing to hand out dates and plans and catastrophe, and the instrument is lost. That is how a contact is corrupted, slowly, and from the inside.

Besides, he says, the details of what may happen to the earth are peripheral. The planet is adjusting to new vibrations, and its surface will shift somewhat. That matters far less than the one question that will be asked of you no matter what happens. Who are you, underneath the illusion. Your inner balance, your identity, your essence, your beingness. That is the only burden to carry into the days to come. For the more of your identity you can fathom, the greater your light will shine in a darkening world.

He borrows words from an old psalm. Yea, though I walk through the valley of death, I shall fear no evil. What matters, he says, is not the valley. What matters is that at each moment, presences guard you, in life and in death. Your consciousness is not subject to death. And those who can shine steadily will be like a lighthouse for others, guiding ships to harbor until they can begin to seek for themselves.

Then comes the line I keep returning to, the one that gave this episode its title. Prepare that part of yourself which shall endure, he says. Prepare not for catastrophe, but for joy. Not for darkness, but for light. Not for fear, but for hope. And never doubt that you are one with many, many brothers and sisters who share with you the hope of love and light for all the peoples of the earth.

Latwii, who speaks after Hatonn, adds something worth sitting with. These are the days the prophets spoke of, he says, and in these days the catalyst is multiplied manyfold. Every upheaval, every fear, every headline, poses the same question to the one who is willing to hear it. What is the meaning of this life in which I see these events. The truth, he says, has never been closer or less veiled to those who seek it. The chaos is not the enemy of awakening. In these years, it is the instrument of it.

There is a resting thought here, and it is this. You did not come here to be told what will happen. You came here to find out who you are, and to shine a little steadier for having found it.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Transparent Veil
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the transparent veil.

Some sessions are fragments. Tonight is one of them. A few hundred words, broken by pauses, with the tape running out mid-thought. What remains is Hatonn, speaking through a new instrument who is still learning the shape of the contact. And yet, inside this fragment, there is a whole philosophy of illusion, packed into a few lines. Sometimes the shortest sessions are the clearest.

Hatonn says he knows how their message sounds. From inside the daily round, from inside the press of your difficulties and trivialities, what they say has a transparent quality. The light of which they speak seems like the illusion, and your problems seem like the solid reality. He admits it outright. The message may seem nearly irrelevant, almost too thin to touch.

And yet, he says, they do not change the message. It is the only message they have. And in their humble opinion, it is the one message which does not partake so heavily of the illusion. It rests, instead, within the framework of that which is not an illusion.

Here is the strange mercy of it, and I love how plainly he puts it. If your experience were transparent to you, if you could see straight through it, you could not learn from it. The solidity is not a cruelty. It is the condition of the lesson. The veil is thick so that you can push against it, and in the pushing, grow.

Think of what it would mean to really believe this. Your day did not feel transparent. The feelings were strong, the patterns of behavior real, the interactions with others weighty. That is as it should be. The lesson wears the costume of reality so that you will take it seriously. Only afterward, in meditation, resting and joined in that quiet vibration, can you begin to see through it, as one would pierce through a veil.

A fragment, then, but a complete one. The world you touch feels solid because it must. The truth you touch feels thin because it is not of this world. And both are doing their work on you at once, the solid teaching you and the transparent reminding you.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Rainbow Beings
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the rainbow beings.

Tonight Hatonn takes up the oldest word in the religious vocabulary, and quietly dismantles it. The word is sin. What he does with it is so gentle that you almost miss the revolution in it. He splits the word in two, keeps one half, and throws the other away entirely.

The half he throws away is the sin of the rulebook. He gives an example, and it is a funny one. In this instrument's mind, he says, it is a sin to wear checked cloth with patterned cloth. That, he says, is an apparent sin which has no meaning whatsoever. And most of what your societies call sinful falls in this category, things with no spiritual reality at all.

The half he keeps is stranger and harder. He asks you to understand yourself as a rainbow being, containing everything. Do you hear of a rapist, he asks. You are he. Do you watch the trial of a murderer. You stand with that person waiting to be sentenced. Whatever you see about you is a mirror to yourself. Each entity is potentially capable of all things. What tests you, and what calls forth your failures, is a function of your biases and your circumstances. But the failure itself is universal. In all cases, he says, it is undeniable that each entity will at some point fail to polarize totally toward service to others. He is not speaking only of the room. He speaks of all those in this density. All will fail, from time to time.

And then the image that makes the whole evening worth keeping. This failure, this sin, is like a child in school who is asked to count two plus two. The child works upon its fingers and says the answer is five. That, Hatonn says, is the nature of what you call sin. It is an error. There is no judgment necessary for an error.

What he asks of you is modest and practical. When you see an error you have made, make note of it, so that at the next testing you may not repeat it. And if you repeat it, you are only exhibiting one hue of a magnificent rainbow. You are still a portion of the Creator. You still hold the birthright of the great wholeness of the white light, and you can at any moment, by an act of will and faith, lift your consciousness out of judgment of self and others and into the vision that sees all things as whole.

Listen to how he closes. Have you looked kindly upon yourself this day, he asks. Have you looked kindly upon others. Have you seen the rainbow. The colors, he says, are so lovely and beautiful, and it is with the greatest love that we rejoice in each of you just as you are, in what you would call an imperfect state.

He says the Christ consciousness, which you may be tempted to place outside yourself in the figure of Jesus, is within you also, just as all the errors and all the mistakes have their place in your being. Why is it so easy to see yourself as sinful, and so hard to see yourself as perfect, when both are true within your language.

I will leave you with his question, because it deserves more than one evening. Have you looked kindly upon yourself this day.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Kindly Grandfather
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the kindly grandfather.

Tonight Latwii answers one of the great questions of the seeker, the one we all ask in some form. Is there something watching over me, or am I on my own. His answer is stranger and warmer than you might expect. There is someone watching. And the someone is you.

He begins with what happens after death, though not the way you would think. There is a review, he says, that takes place in what he calls the density of eight. It is not a courtroom. No one sits across from you and reads out your failings. Instead, the incarnation just passed is bathed in white light, and the learnings are seen within the wholeness of the love and light of the one Creator. The light itself is the review. You see your life illuminated, and the further needs for learning become clear, and the decisions for the next incarnation are made.

Then the part I love. The one you call the higher self, he says, exists within the sixth density. And its relationship to you is like that of a kindly grandfather overseeing the progress of his grandchild. This grandfather provides the blueprint, the framework of the lessons you came to learn. But you, the grandchild, choose freely how to learn them, at what speed, and you embellish upon them as it meets your fancy. That last phrase is so good. You are allowed to embellish.

Time, he says, is the confusing part. You live inside the illusion of past and future. But if you could see all of it at once, it would look like a solid sphere of infinite proportions, and the path of your evolution could be chosen at any point, in any direction. The linearity is only how the journey looks from inside one lifetime. Your higher self is not waiting for you in the future. It is with you now, in a larger sense of now.

And you are not a single thing, but portions of yourself distributed across the densities, resources and guides you can call upon at any point in the incarnation, and most especially between incarnations, for guidance in the further learning of lessons. Each entity, he says, has these resources. They are yours to call on. A simple request in meditation is all that is necessary.

A kindly grandfather, then, not a judge. A blueprint, not a chain. And the white light of review, waiting patiently at the end of every life, to show you what you learned and what remains to learn.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Lesson of the Squirrel
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the lesson of the squirrel.

Tonight Hatonn tells a story about a squirrel. It is a small story, and I do not think you will forget it. The squirrel, he says, spends its life storing food for the winter. It is serious-minded, not prone to relax and let the universe provide. It works constantly, taking responsibility for its own sustenance, trusting the future to no one. Many would call it insignificant, even an object of prey. But Hatonn sees a teacher.

The squirrel, he says, is like those who strive upon a spiritual path. The elder squirrels will not let the world provide for them. They constantly strive to improve their situation, gathering what is available at the moment, no matter how unnecessary it may seem. For they know that what seems of questionable value today may be perceived, at a later date, as a jewel beyond comparison.

Here is where the story turns its teeth on you, and I mean that as praise. It is convenient, he says, to glance around at what life is offering and tell yourself that you do not need to learn this. That it is of no use to you at this moment. That later, at a more convenient time, when the education appears more valuable, you will begin. The difficulty with this attitude is that when the need arrives, it arrives at a critical time. It does not wait for you to get ready. The later date will be thrust upon you, born with the force of your indolence, and the lesson will come coupled with another lesson, the lesson of your reluctance to learn.

So do not take the gifts and put them on the shelf until the ideal moment. The arrival of a lesson, he says, is itself the signal. You summoned it. It comes at the point in your life which is the ideal condition for it, whether you recognize it or not. The ideal time is now, disguised as the inconvenient time.

And then the sentence that quietly crowns the whole discourse. He says this not to chastise, for you are deeply loved, and it is not his place to correct your path. For there is but one teacher on each of your paths. That teacher is yourself.
